note: Every answer carries an explanation, including correct ones.

questions.stem: You own 100 shares of a commercial bank. In what two ways can that holding actually pay you?

options.t: Dividends from the company, and a higher price paid by another investor
Interest paid monthly by NEPSE, and dividends
Rent from the bank's branches, and capital gains
Dividends, and a guaranteed buyback at face value

questions.explain: Only two channels exist. The company distributes part of its profit to you as a cash dividend or bonus shares; or another investor buys your shares for more than you paid. NEPSE pays no interest — it operates the market, it does not hold your money. There is no guaranteed buyback, and nothing about Rs. 100 face value creates a floor under the price.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Think about who can actually send money in your direction: the company, or another investor.

questions.stem: Which of these are genuinely unavailable to a retail investor on NEPSE? (Select all that apply)

options.t: Short selling a share you do not own
Buying a call option on a listed bank
Buying and selling the same share within one day
Placing an order outside market hours

questions.explain: NEPSE is an order-driven cash equity market. There is no short selling, no options or futures, and no intraday trading — the last one follows structurally from T+2 settlement, because you cannot sell shares that have not yet reached your Demat account. Placing an order outside market hours IS possible since April 2026: orders can be entered round the clock, they simply queue and execute only between 11:00 and 15:00.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these are structural absences on NEPSE. One of them changed in April 2026.

questions.stem: A bank has 8.6 crore shares outstanding at the standard Nepali face value. What is its paid-up capital, in crore rupees?
questions.explain: Paid-up capital = share count × face value = 8.6 crore × Rs. 100 = Rs. 860 crore. Face value for Nepali ordinary shares is Rs. 100 (mutual fund units are Rs. 10). Note what this figure is not: it has no relationship to the market price. The same bank could trade at Rs. 200 or Rs. 600 and its paid-up capital would be unchanged.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Paid-up capital uses face value, not market price. What is face value for a Nepali ordinary share?

questions.stem: Why do Nepali banks pay so much of their dividend as bonus shares rather than cash?

options.t: It raises paid-up capital to meet NRB minimums without asking shareholders for new money
Bonus shares are taxed at a lower rate than cash dividends for the company
SEBON requires at least half of any dividend to be paid in shares
It increases the market value of the shareholders' holding

questions.explain: Nepal Rastra Bank sets minimum paid-up capital by licence class. A bonus issue moves money from reserves into the capital column, satisfying the requirement without a cash call on shareholders. The other options are wrong in instructive ways: there is no such SEBON rule; and a bonus issue does not increase the value of your holding — your share count rises and the price adjusts down by roughly the same proportion on the ex-bonus date. You own more pieces of the same pie.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Ask what problem the bank is solving. Who requires it to hold a certain amount of capital?

questions.stem: You buy 200 kitta of a hydropower company on NEPSE at Rs. 300. Where does your Rs. 60,000 go?

options.t: To the investor who sold you the shares — the company receives nothing
To the company, to fund construction of the project
Split between the company and the selling investor
To NEPSE, which passes it to the company at settlement

questions.explain: This is a secondary-market transaction. The shares already exist and you are buying them from another investor, who receives your money less their own costs. The company is not a party to the trade and its bank balance is unaffected. Money reaches the company only through the primary market — an IPO, FPO or rights issue. This distinction matters when you read that a company 'gained Rs. 50 crore in market value': that phrase describes an opinion changing, not a rupee moving into the business.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Were these shares newly created by the company, or did they already exist in someone else's Demat account?

questions.stem: The main purpose of the secondary market is to raise capital for listed companies.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False. The secondary market raises no capital for companies at all — it provides two other things: a price, and an exit. Those are what make the primary market work. You are willing to buy at an IPO partly because you know you can sell later; without a functioning secondary market almost nobody would fund the primary one. So the secondary market is essential to capital formation without itself forming any capital.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Think about who receives the money in a secondary-market trade.

questions.stem: NMB trades at Rs. 233.00 with EPS of Rs. 17.10. Citizens Bank trades at Rs. 194.60 with EPS of Rs. 4.63. Which is the more expensive share?

options.t: Citizens Bank — you pay 30.45× earnings versus NMB's 15.35×
NMB — it costs Rs. 38.40 more per share
They are equally priced once you account for face value
Citizens Bank, because it trades further above its Rs. 100 face value

questions.explain: You are buying earnings, not a price tag. CZBIL at Rs. 194.60 on EPS of Rs. 4.63 is a P/E of 30.45×; NMB at Rs. 233.00 on EPS of Rs. 17.10 is 15.35×. Per Rs. 1,000 invested, NMB buys you Rs. 73.39 of annual earnings against CZBIL's Rs. 23.80 — and NMB's ROE of 10.34% against CZBIL's 3.14% says the business is far better at using capital too. The lower sticker price belongs to the more expensive share.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Divide the price by the earnings per share for each, and compare those two numbers instead of the prices.

questions.stem: A share is trading at Rs. 89, below its Rs. 100 face value. What does that tell you?

options.t: That the market values the company below the capital put into it — which is usually a judgement, not a bargain
That the share is cheap, because it is below face value
That the company must buy the shares back at Rs. 100
Nothing at all — face value and market price are unrelated in every way

questions.explain: Trading below face value tells you the market thinks the company is worth less than the paid-in capital — often because earnings have collapsed or are negative, as with Laxmi Sunrise at an EPS of −Rs. 2.04. That is a judgement about the business, not a discount. No buyback obligation exists at face value. The last option overcorrects: the two numbers are genuinely different measures, but the relationship between price and paid-in capital does carry information — it just is not the information beginners read into it.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: If a company earns nothing, is a low price a bargain or an assessment?

questions.stem: The NEPSE index peaked at 3,198.60 on 18 August 2021 and fell to 1,615 by early 2023. What was the drawdown, as a percentage? Enter a positive number.
questions.explain: (3,198.60 − 1,615) ÷ 3,198.60 = 49.5%. That is the diversified index — a basket of every listed company. Individual stocks in the same period fell considerably further. Recovering a 49.5% loss requires a gain of 98.1%, which is the arithmetic of Lesson 14.4: G = L ÷ (1 − L).
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Measure the fall against the peak, not against the trough.

questions.stem: Someone who invested Rs. 1,00,000 at the August 2021 peak and held to today (index 2,643.83) is:

options.t: Down about 17%, five years later
Roughly back to break-even
Up about 64%, because the market recovered from the 2023 trough
Down about 50%, because that was the size of the crash

questions.explain: 2,643.83 ÷ 3,198.60 = 0.827, so the holding is worth about Rs. 82,655 — down 17.3%. The +63.7% figure is real but belongs to someone who bought at the 1,615 trough, not the peak. And the −49.5% was the maximum drawdown, from which the index has partly recovered. The lesson underneath: the price you pay determines your return, and 'long-term investor' has meant five years and counting for whoever bought the top.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Compare today's index directly against the index level on the day they bought.

questions.stem: Which factors have driven every NEPSE boom-and-bust cycle? (Select all that apply)

options.t: Interest rates
Liquidity in the banking system
How easy it was for new people to open accounts
Changes to the capital gains tax rate

questions.explain: The same three ingredients appear in different proportions in each cycle: interest rates, banking-system liquidity, and the ease of new-account opening. The 2019–2021 run had all three at maximum — NRB had cut rates, the system was flush, and MeroShare plus online trading had removed the friction from opening an account. Capital gains tax changed in July 2026, well after all four cycles, and has never been a cycle driver.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these are macro and structural. One is a tax change that happened in 2026.

questions.stem: Your broker has not paid your sale proceeds three weeks after settlement and has stopped responding. Where does your complaint go?

options.t: SEBON — the regulator, which licenses brokers and takes enforcement action
NEPSE — it operates the market the broker trades on
CDSC — it holds the shares that were sold
Nepal Rastra Bank — it regulates financial institutions

questions.explain: SEBON licenses brokers and has enforcement powers over them; complaints go there, in writing, with your client code, trade date and contract note. NEPSE operates the market but does not discipline brokers. CDSC is the depository and holds shares, not money. NRB regulates banks and monetary policy, not securities brokers. This catches people constantly because NEPSE is the name everyone knows.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which of these four bodies licenses brokers and can take enforcement action against one?

questions.stem: Nepal deliberately separates trading (NEPSE/TMS) from custody (CDSC/MeroShare). What does that separation buy you, and what does it cost you?

options.t: It protects your shares if a broker fails — and it costs you the EDIS step on every sale
It makes settlement faster — and it costs you a higher DP charge
It lowers commission — and it costs you the ability to trade intraday
It is purely historical and has no practical consequence today

questions.explain: Your shares sit in your own Demat account at CDSC, not in your broker's custody — so a broker failure does not put your holdings at risk. The price of that protection is that nobody, not even the exchange, can move shares out of your account without your authorisation. That authorisation is EDIS, submitted in MeroShare on T+1, and skipping it fails the sale. Intraday is impossible because of T+2 settlement, not because of this separation.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: If nobody else can reach into your Demat account, who has to authorise a delivery when you sell?

questions.stem: Put these five institutions in the order your money and shares encounter them when you buy shares for the first time.
items: Your bank — you transfer funds via ConnectIPS
Your broker — receives the funds and routes your order
NEPSE — matches your order against a seller
CDSC — clears the trade and moves the shares
Your DP — the Demat account where the shares are credited
questions.explain: Money starts at your bank, moves to the broker's collection account, and the broker routes your order to NEPSE, which matches it. CDSC then clears the trade, and the shares are credited to your Demat account, which your DP maintains on CDSC's behalf. Notice that the broker never holds your shares at any point — that is the custody separation doing its job.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Follow the money first, then follow the shares back.

questions.stem: How many of NEPSE's 271 listed companies are hydropower companies?
questions.explain: 91 of 271, or 33.6% — a third of the exchange by company count, and by far the largest sector. Microfinance is second with 50 (18.5%). But company count is not market weight: the 19 commercial banks are only 7.0% of the count and dominate the capitalisation-weighted index, which is why the headline NEPSE number mostly reflects what the banks did.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: It is roughly a third of the 271 listed companies.

questions.stem: You buy NABIL, NMB, SANIMA, GBIME and PCBL, reasoning that five companies is diversified. What have you actually built?

options.t: Close to a single position — Nepali commercial banks correlate at roughly 0.90
A well-diversified portfolio, since these are five separate companies
A hedged portfolio, because some banks gain when others lose
A diversified portfolio, because they have different P/E ratios

questions.explain: All five fund themselves the same way, lend into the same economy and reprice together the morning NRB changes a rule. Nepali commercial banks correlate at roughly 0.86–0.91, so five names behave close to one position. Different P/E ratios reflect different earnings, not different risk drivers. The genuine diversifier on NEPSE is hydropower at around 0.62 — which is awkward, because it is also the least liquid part of the exchange.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Ask what would happen to all five on the morning Nepal Rastra Bank tightens the credit-to-deposit ratio.

questions.stem: The headline NEPSE index rises 1.4% while the Sensitive Index rises only 0.35%. What is that telling you?

options.t: Smaller, lower-quality names are leading the move
The Group A companies are being accumulated by institutions
One of the two indices has a calculation error
Promoter shares are being converted to public shares

questions.explain: The Sensitive Index covers Group A companies only — the larger, better-disclosed names. When the all-company index outruns it, the money is going into the tail rather than the leaders. That is one of the three reliable warning signs in Lesson 15.1, alongside accelerating new-account growth and rising leverage. One day of it means nothing; a month of it is a reason to reduce position size and stop adding.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What does the Sensitive Index include that the headline index does not restrict itself to?

questions.stem: What does the Float Index exclude that the headline NEPSE index does not?

options.t: Promoter and locked-in shares — it weights only shares actually available to trade
Companies outside Group A
Hydropower companies, because of their thin volume
Companies with negative earnings

questions.explain: The Float Index weights by free float — the shares genuinely available for trading — so it excludes promoter holdings and locked-in shares. It is arguably the most honest measure of what the investable market did, because it gives no weight to shares nobody can buy. Restricting to Group A is what the Sensitive Index does; neither index filters by sector or by earnings.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The clue is in the word 'float'. Which shares are not actually floating?

questions.stem: NEPSE trades Sunday through Thursday.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False. Since April 2026 NEPSE trades Monday to Friday, 11:00–15:00, following the change in government office days. It ran Sunday–Thursday for its entire prior history, which is why nearly every tutorial published before 2026 says so — and why this catches people. Saturday and Sunday are now market holidays. This matters practically: settlement counts trading days, so a Thursday sale settles on Monday.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Something about the trading week changed in April 2026.

questions.stem: The NEPSE index falls 5.2% ninety minutes after the open. What happens?

options.t: Trading halts for 15 minutes
The market closes for the day
Nothing — 5% only triggers a halt in the final hour
Trading halts for 15 minutes and reopens with a ±5% band

questions.explain: Since 21 April 2026 the index circuit breaker has two tiers, not three: a 5% move within the first two hours halts trading for 15 minutes, and an 8% move at any time closes the market for the day. Ninety minutes is inside the first two hours, so this is the Level 1 halt. Note this is entirely separate from the ±15% daily limit on an individual stock — two different mechanisms, both live at once.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: There are two tiers since April 2026. Which one applies within the first two hours?

questions.stem: Since April 2026 you can place an order on NEPSE at 22:00 and it will execute immediately.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: Half true, which is why it is worth asking. You genuinely can place orders round the clock since April 2026 — that part is new and useful. But they only queue; execution happens exclusively during the 11:00–15:00 session. The practical benefit is real: you can decide your maximum price calmly the night before rather than at 11:04 with the market moving, which is precisely the discipline Lesson 5.1 asks for.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Placing and executing are two different things. Which one is round the clock?

questions.stem: An IPO closes in two days and you have a bank account but nothing else. Can you apply?

options.t: No — you need a Demat account first, and it takes days to open
Yes — you can apply through your bank's C-ASBA counter directly
Yes — a broker can apply on your behalf using your citizenship certificate
Yes, but only for the minimum 10 units

questions.explain: The Demat account is the gating step: C-ASBA applications go through MeroShare, which exists only once you have a Demat with a DP, and opening one typically takes several days. No broker or bank can apply on your behalf without it, and there is no minimum-lot exception. This is the practical reason to open your accounts in a quiet week rather than when you have a reason to hurry.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Where do allotted shares get credited? You need that thing to exist first.

questions.stem: Put the four accounts in the order you must set them up.
items: Demat account with a DP — you receive a 16-digit BOID
questions.explain: Each step depends on the one before. The bank account funds everything. The Demat must exist before MeroShare credentials can be issued for it. And while a broker account can technically be opened in parallel, you cannot fund it or use it meaningfully without the rest. Total realistic time from nothing to your first order: one to two weeks.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which account do the others all reference?

questions.stem: Which of these is a genuine reason to prefer one DP over another?

options.t: How responsive they are when an EDIS authorisation fails on a T+1 afternoon
How safely they hold your shares
The DP charge they levy per settlement
Whether they can get you better prices on NEPSE

questions.explain: Every DP holds your shares in exactly the same place — CDSC's system — so safety is not a differentiator. The Rs. 25 DP charge is regulated and identical everywhere. No DP influences execution prices; that is NEPSE's matching engine. What genuinely differs is the annual maintenance charge and, far more importantly, whether someone answers when a delivery authorisation fails on the one afternoon it matters.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these are identical at every DP by regulation or by design.

questions.stem: You buy 100 kitta of NABIL in the morning and another 150 kitta of NABIL in the afternoon of the same day. How much DP charge do you pay?

options.t: Rs. 25 — it is per company per settlement date, not per trade
Rs. 50 — two separate trades
Rs. 25 per 100 kitta, so Rs. 62.50
Nothing — DP charge applies only when you sell

questions.explain: The DP charge is Rs. 25 per company per settlement date. Both purchases are the same company on the same day, so they settle together and attract one charge. This has a real consequence in the other direction: if a single order fills partially across two days, it settles twice and you pay Rs. 25 twice — which is a small but genuine argument for placing orders you expect to fill completely.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Read the basis carefully: per what, per what?

questions.stem: What is the WACC figure shown in your MeroShare portfolio?

options.t: Your average per-share purchase cost — the basis your capital gains tax is computed against
The current market value of your holding
The weighted average price the stock traded at today
An estimate of what the shares are worth, updated monthly

questions.explain: WACC is your weighted average cost across all lots — what you paid, on average, per share. It is the official cost basis for capital gains tax, which is withheld at source on the difference between your net sale proceeds and WACC × quantity. People routinely misread it as market value and reach exactly the wrong conclusion about whether they are up or down. If your WACC looks wrong after a bonus, rights issue or transfer, fix it with your DP before you sell.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The C in WACC stands for cost. Whose cost, and when was it incurred?

questions.stem: You hold 200 kitta with a WACC of Rs. 498.02. You receive a 15% bonus issue. What is your new WACC, in rupees?
questions.explain: Your total cost is unchanged at 200 × 498.02 = Rs. 99,604. A 15% bonus gives you 230 shares. New WACC = 99,604 ÷ 230 = Rs. 433.06. You are not richer — the same money now sits across more shares, and the market price adjusted down on the ex-bonus date by roughly the same proportion. What has changed is your future tax bill: sell at Rs. 500 later and the gain is computed against Rs. 433.06, not Rs. 498.02. Bonus shares defer tax; they do not avoid it.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Your total cost does not change. Only the number of shares it is divided by.

questions.stem: Your order shows in the TMS order book with status 'Open'. What do you own?

options.t: Nothing yet — an open order has not executed
The full quantity you ordered
Half the quantity, pending settlement
The shares, but they are locked until T+2

questions.explain: The order book shows what you have submitted; the trade book shows what has actually executed. An 'Open' order is sitting in the queue at your price and may never fill at all — which is not a bug, it is you refusing to overpay. Only rows in the trade book mean shares. Confusing the two books is the most common TMS mistake, and it leads people to miscount their position.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which of the two books lists trades that actually happened?

questions.stem: Which statements about TMS orders are true? (Select all that apply)

options.t: Every order must name a price — there is no market order
Orders are day orders and expire at the close
Orders can be entered outside session hours and will queue
You can set a good-till-cancelled order that stays live for a week

questions.explain: NEPSE offers limit orders only, and they are day orders — an order you placed on Monday is gone by Tuesday morning and it is on you to place it again. There is no good-till-cancelled. What did change in April 2026 is that orders can be entered round the clock; they simply queue and execute only between 11:00 and 15:00.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these are true. The false one describes an order type NEPSE does not offer.

questions.stem: You see a price you want at 11:02 and start a ConnectIPS transfer to your broker at 11:03. Can you buy at 11:04?

options.t: No — funds must be cleared in the broker's account before you can place a buy order
Yes — the broker extends intraday credit against a pending transfer
Yes, up to 50% of the transfer value as margin
Yes, but only for Group A companies

questions.explain: NEPSE gives you no margin, no overdraft and no credit — funds must be in and cleared before you can buy. This is a genuine constraint on how you operate: fund the account at the start of the week you intend to buy. It is also a real protection. You cannot lose more than you have committed, and there is no margin call to force you out at the worst possible moment.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Does the exchange lend you anything at all?

questions.stem: When you apply for an IPO through C-ASBA, the application money leaves your bank account immediately.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False, and this is one of the genuinely well-designed parts of the Nepali system. C-ASBA means Centralised Application Supported by Blocked Amount: the money is blocked in your own bank account, not debited. If you are not allotted, the block is simply released — the money never left, and you keep any interest it earned. It is only debited if and when shares are actually allotted to you.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What does the 'BA' in ASBA stand for?

questions.stem: UPPER closed yesterday at Rs. 230.00 and is trading at Rs. 236.00 now. Which reference price does the ±15% daily circuit use?

options.t: The previous close of Rs. 230.00 — giving Rs. 195.50 to Rs. 264.50
The last traded price of Rs. 236.00 — giving Rs. 200.60 to Rs. 271.40
The day's opening price
The weighted average of today's trades so far

questions.explain: The daily circuit is measured from the previous close and is fixed for the whole day: Rs. 230 × 0.85 = Rs. 195.50 and Rs. 230 × 1.15 = Rs. 264.50. The LTP is the reference for the other limit — the ±3% order price band, which moves as the stock moves. Two limits, two reference prices, both live at once, and mixing them up is the most common reason a beginner's order gets rejected.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: One limit is fixed for the day and one moves with the price. Which is which?

questions.stem: Why does NEPSE compute its closing price as a weighted average of late trades rather than taking the final tick?

options.t: So a single small trade in the last seconds cannot set tomorrow's circuit reference
To make the index easier to compute
Because the final tick is often a block trade
To smooth the index for reporting purposes

questions.explain: The close sets tomorrow's ±15% circuit reference, so it is a consequential number. Using a weighted average of the last portion of the session's trades means one small order in the final seconds cannot move it — which would otherwise be a cheap way to manipulate the following day's permitted range. On a liquid bank the difference from the LTP is trivial; on a thin counter it can matter.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What important thing does tomorrow depend on the close for?

questions.stem: A hydropower stock shows a best bid of Rs. 296.00 and a best ask of Rs. 305.00. You buy at the ask and immediately sell at the bid. Ignoring commission, what is your loss?
questions.explain: You buy at 305 and sell at 296, losing Rs. 9 on a Rs. 305 outlay = 2.95%. The 3.04% answer computes the same Rs. 9 against the bid of Rs. 296 instead of against what you actually paid — your loss is always measured against your outlay. This spread alone is roughly nine times the buy-side commission: on thin NEPSE counters the spread, not the commission, is your dominant cost.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Divide the Rs. 9 loss by the price you actually paid, not by the price you sold at.

questions.stem: You are choosing between two counters with identical charts. One has a 0.1% spread, the other 3%. What does that difference mean in practice?

options.t: The 3% counter costs you 3% in round-trip damage before the price has moved at all
The 3% counter is more volatile and therefore more profitable
Nothing — the spread is a fee that goes to the broker either way
The 3% counter has higher commission

questions.explain: The spread is not a fee anyone charges you — it is the cost of insisting on trading immediately, and it is paid once getting in and once getting out. A 3% spread means the price must move 3% in your favour before you are level, on top of commission, SEBON fee and DP charge. Commission rates are regulated and identical across counters. A wide spread signals thin liquidity, which is also what makes any technical signal on that counter less reliable.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: You pay the spread twice — once entering, once leaving.

questions.stem: A stock shows Rs. 2 crore of turnover today across just 3 transactions. What does that most likely indicate?

options.t: A block trade between institutions, not market interest
Very strong retail demand for the stock
A data error, since turnover that high needs more trades
That the stock hit its circuit limit

questions.explain: Rs. 2 crore across 3 transactions means an average trade of about Rs. 66.7 lakh — that is two or three institutions agreeing a block, not a market. The same Rs. 2 crore across 4,000 transactions would mean hundreds of participants and genuine depth you could trade into. Turnover alone hides the shape of the day, which is why you read volume, turnover and transaction count together.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Divide the turnover by the number of transactions and ask who trades in that size.

questions.stem: A counter averages Rs. 2,00,000 of daily turnover. You hold a Rs. 2,00,000 position and assume you can be at most 10% of a day's turnover when exiting. How many trading days to get out?
questions.explain: 10% of Rs. 2,00,000 is Rs. 20,000 you can realistically sell per day. Rs. 2,00,000 ÷ Rs. 20,000 = 10 trading days — two full weeks. Any bad news reaches the price long before you reach the door, which means your stop loss on this counter is a wish rather than a plan. Nothing on the chart tells you this; the volume column is where the risk is written down, and it is the column most people skip.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: First work out how much you can sell in one day, then divide.

questions.stem: Which is measured in rupees rather than shares?

options.t: Turnover
Volume
Transactions
Kitta

questions.explain: Turnover is the rupee value traded — price × volume. Volume is the number of shares, expressed in kitta. Transactions is a count of separate trades. The distinction matters because the same volume means very different amounts of money at different price levels: 10,000 kitta of a Rs. 89 share is Rs. 8.9 lakh, while 10,000 kitta of Everest Bank at Rs. 670 is Rs. 67 lakh.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: One of these four words is the Nepali term for a single share.

questions.stem: What can the floorsheet genuinely tell you? (Select all that apply)

options.t: Whether a day's buying was concentrated in one broker or spread widely
Whether a price move had broad participation
Which individual person bought the shares
What the buyer intends to do next

questions.explain: The floorsheet lists buying broker, selling broker, quantity and rate for every executed trade, so concentration and participation are directly readable. What it cannot give you is identity or intent: one broker has thousands of clients, so heavy buying through broker 58 tells you about a broker, not a person. And concentrated accumulation looks identical whether it is a coordinated pump or an institution building a legitimate position.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Look at the four columns the floorsheet actually publishes. What is not in them?

questions.stem: A counter runs 20% in nine sessions, turnover rises sixfold, and three brokers account for 78% of the buying. What is the correct response?

options.t: Treat it as a reason for scepticism about any tip that arrives next — not as a trade signal
Buy, because concentrated accumulation means informed money is entering
Report it to SEBON immediately as market manipulation
Ignore it — broker concentration is meaningless

questions.explain: Concentration is real information, but it shows you concentration and not intent. This is the shape of the accumulation phase of a pump; it is also the exact shape of one institution building a legitimate position or a fund rebalancing. You cannot tell from the sheet, and you are always reading it after the fact. Its honest value is defensive: when a tip about this counter arrives three days later, you already know the buying was concentrated — and that scepticism is worth more than any trade you would make from it.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Does the floorsheet distinguish a pump from a fund rebalancing?

questions.stem: The NEPSE floorsheet is privileged information available only to brokers.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False. The floorsheet is published daily and publicly on nepalstock.com, and Sharesansar and Merolagani aggregate it by broker into a far more readable form. Nothing in it is privileged — everyone can see it, including the people whose trades are in it. That is worth remembering when someone offers you 'inside information' derived from it.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Where does NEPSE publish it?

questions.stem: You place a buy limit order at Rs. 240. The stock trades between Rs. 243 and Rs. 251 all day. What happens?

options.t: Nothing fills — and that is the order working correctly
It fills at Rs. 243, the lowest price of the day
It fills at Rs. 251, the closing price
It converts to a market order at the close

questions.explain: A buy limit at Rs. 240 means 'buy for me at Rs. 240 or less, never more'. The stock never traded at or below Rs. 240, so nothing filled. That is not a malfunction — it is you refusing to overpay, which is the correct behaviour. NEPSE has no market orders and no mechanism that converts an unfilled limit into one; the order simply expires at the close, because NEPSE orders are day orders.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What does the word 'limit' actually promise you?

questions.stem: UPPER closed yesterday at Rs. 230.00 and is currently trading at Rs. 236.00. Which order will be rejected?
questions.explain: Two limits apply at once. The daily circuit is ±15% of the previous close (Rs. 195.50–264.50), so Rs. 210 is inside it. But the order price band is ±3% of the last traded price of Rs. 236.00, giving Rs. 228.92–243.08. Rs. 210 is outside that band and is rejected. Rs. 229.50, Rs. 234.00 and Rs. 242.00 all sit inside both limits. The band follows the price during the day; the circuit does not.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Work out both ranges: ±15% of Rs. 230, and ±3% of Rs. 236. Which order fails one of them?

questions.stem: You and another investor both bid Rs. 240 for the same stock. They placed their order four seconds before you. What happens when 200 kitta are offered at Rs. 240?

options.t: They fill first — every share — because matching is by price then time
The 200 kitta are split equally between you
The larger order fills first
They are allocated proportionally to order size

questions.explain: NEPSE matches by price–time priority. At the same price, whoever arrived first fills first — completely, before the next order in the queue gets anything. There is no pro-rata allocation and size confers no advantage. This is why modifying an order's price is expensive: the modified order goes to the back of the queue for its new price, which Lesson 5.5 covers.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Price first, then what?

questions.stem: What is the usual minimum order quantity on NEPSE, in kitta?
questions.explain: Ten kitta, in multiples of ten. Odd lots — quantities that do not fit the lot size, often created when a bonus issue leaves you with 137 shares instead of 140 — trade in a separate market with much thinner liquidity. Plan to sell the round lot and expect the odd remainder to be difficult to clear at a good price.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: It is the same number as the minimum units in a fixed-price IPO.

questions.stem: You place an order on Monday and it does not fill. What is its status on Tuesday morning?

options.t: Gone — NEPSE orders are day orders and expire at the close
Still live, until you cancel it
Still live for seven days, then it expires
Automatically re-entered at the same price

questions.explain: NEPSE orders are day orders. They expire at the close and nothing re-enters them for you — it is on you to place the order again. There is no good-till-cancelled order type. What did change in April 2026 is that you may now enter orders round the clock; they queue and execute only during the 11:00–15:00 session, which lets you set your price calmly the night before.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: How long does a NEPSE order live?

questions.stem: In the pre-open session, you bid Rs. 237 and the equilibrium price is discovered at Rs. 231. What do you pay?

options.t: Rs. 231 — every crossing order executes at the single discovered price
Rs. 237, the price you bid
The average of Rs. 231 and Rs. 237
Nothing — your bid was too far above the equilibrium

questions.explain: Pre-open collects orders without matching, then computes one equilibrium price that maximises executable volume. Every crossing order fills at that single price. Your limit is a ceiling, so bidding Rs. 237 means you were willing to pay up to Rs. 237 — and the auction found Rs. 231, which is better for you. This is the closest NEPSE gets to a market order, and on a liquid stock it is a reasonable way to enter.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: How many prices does a single-price auction produce?

questions.stem: How wide is the pre-open price band, and from what is it measured?

options.t: ±5% of the previous close
±3% of the last traded price
±15% of the previous close
±2% of the previous close

questions.explain: The pre-open band is ±5% of the previous close, raised from ±2% in the 2026 rule changes. It is a third limit, distinct from the ±3% continuous-session band (measured from the last traded price) and the ±15% daily circuit (measured from the previous close). All three widened at once in 2026, so any source quoting ±2% predates the change.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three bands exist. This one is wider than the continuous-session band but much narrower than the daily circuit.

questions.stem: Your order book shows 'Partially executed — 180 of 500 filled'. Your trade book shows one row. How many shares do you own?

options.t: 180, and they settle on T+2
500 — the order was accepted in full
None until the whole order fills
320, the unfilled remainder

questions.explain: Only executed quantity means shares, and only the trade book records executions. 180 filled, so 180 are yours and will settle into your Demat on T+2. The remaining 320 stay live in the order book and will expire at the close if they do not fill. Confusing the two books is the most common TMS mistake and leads people to miscount their position.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which of the two books records what actually happened?

questions.stem: A single order fills 180 kitta on Monday and 320 kitta on Tuesday, all in the same company. What is the total DP charge, in rupees?
questions.explain: Rs. 50. The DP charge is Rs. 25 per company per settlement date, and two fill days means two settlement dates. Had the whole order filled on one day it would have been Rs. 25. Note what does not change: commission and SEBON fee are proportional, so they are the same either way. Only the flat charge doubles — which is a real, if small, argument for placing orders you expect to fill completely.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The charge is per company per settlement date. How many settlement dates are there here?

questions.stem: Modifying an open order's price keeps your position in the time queue.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False. Matching is by price then time, and a modified order re-enters the book at the back of the queue for its new price. This matters most in exactly the situation where people reach for the modify button — a fast-moving, well-bid stock where the queue at each level is long. Reducing quantity generally preserves your place; the safe assumption is that any modification sends you to the back.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: If changing your price kept your place, everyone would do it constantly. Why would that break the queue?

questions.stem: Which of these is a good reason to cancel a resting buy order?

options.t: Nepal Rastra Bank published a circular that changes your view of the sector
The price moved away from you and you want to chase it
It has been open for two hours without filling
Another stock looks like it is moving faster today

questions.explain: Cancel when the reason you wanted the stock has changed — new information, a change in your circumstances, or a realisation that you sized the position wrong. Do not cancel merely because the price moved away: that is chasing, and it is how you end up paying a price you had already decided was too high. An order open for two hours is simply an order doing its job. Decide your maximum before you log in, and let the order live or die at that price.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which option describes new information, and which three describe impatience?

questions.stem: You can cancel the portion of your order that has already executed.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False. An executed portion is a completed trade with its own contract note, its own commission, its own DP charge and — when you eventually sell it — its own capital gains tax computed from its own lot. Only the unfilled remainder can be cancelled. Unwinding an execution means a fresh sale with a fresh round of costs.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Once a trade has happened, is there anything left to cancel?

questions.stem: You sell shares on Thursday 20 August 2026. On which day does the trade settle?

options.t: Monday 24 August
Saturday 22 August
Friday 21 August
Tuesday 25 August

questions.explain: T+2 counts trading days, not calendar days. Since April 2026 NEPSE trades Monday to Friday, so Saturday and Sunday are market holidays. Thursday (T) → Friday (T+1) → Monday (T+2). Add a further day or two for your broker to move the net proceeds to your bank. If you need cash by a specific date, count backwards in trading days and check the holiday calendar — Dashain and Tihar extend it considerably.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Count two TRADING days forward from Thursday. Which days does NEPSE trade?

questions.stem: You buy shares on Monday. When do they appear in your Demat account?

options.t: Wednesday — T+2
Immediately on execution
Tuesday — T+1
When you authorise EDIS

questions.explain: Shares are credited on T+2, which for a Monday purchase is Wednesday. On T the trade exists but the shares do not; T+1 is clearing. EDIS is a seller's obligation, not a buyer's — when you buy, the process is passive and there is nothing for you to do. This is also why intraday trading is impossible: you cannot sell what has not yet reached your account.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which day of the settlement cycle actually moves shares?

questions.stem: You sold shares and the trade shows as executed in TMS. What must you do next, and when?

options.t: Authorise EDIS in MeroShare on T+1, using your Demat transaction PIN
Nothing — the broker handles delivery
Transfer the shares to your broker's account in TMS
Confirm the sale in TMS on T+2

questions.explain: Nepal separates trading (NEPSE, via TMS) from custody (CDSC, via MeroShare), and nobody — not your broker, not the exchange — can move shares out of your Demat without your authorisation. EDIS is that authorisation, submitted in MeroShare on T+1 with your Demat transaction PIN. Your broker cannot do it for you. Skipping it sends the trade to auction settlement, and the cost lands on you.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Who is the only person who can release shares from your own Demat account?

questions.stem: Put these in the correct order for selling shares on NEPSE.
items: Place the sell order in TMS
The order executes — visible in your trade book
On T+1, authorise EDIS in MeroShare with your transaction PIN
On T+2, shares are delivered and funds settle net of CGT
Your broker transfers the net proceeds to your bank
questions.explain: Step 3 is the one people omit. Nepal separates trading (NEPSE/TMS) from custody (CDSC/MeroShare), and EDIS is the bridge between them — nobody can move shares out of your Demat but you. Skipping it leads to auction settlement: NEPSE buys the shares in the market to deliver to your buyer, and charges you the difference plus a penalty.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Two of these happen in TMS, two involve settlement, and one is the step almost everyone forgets.

questions.stem: You sold 300 kitta at Rs. 356.90 and forgot to authorise EDIS. The auction buys the shares at an average of Rs. 374.50. Roughly what does the failure cost you, before any penalty?

options.t: About Rs. 5,280 — the price difference on 300 shares
Nothing — the buyer bears the cost
Rs. 374.50, a flat auction fee
The full sale value of Rs. 1,07,070

questions.explain: 300 × (374.50 − 356.90) = Rs. 5,280, plus a penalty on top. NEPSE buys the shares in the open market to deliver to your buyer, and you pay whatever that costs above your sale price. Note the asymmetry: had the stock fallen instead, the auction would have bought cheaply and you would NOT have received the difference. You bear the downside and keep none of the upside — which is exactly why the two-minute EDIS task matters.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Multiply the price difference by the quantity the auction had to buy.

questions.stem: Why is intraday trading impossible on NEPSE?

options.t: Shares arrive on T+2, so you cannot sell what you do not yet hold
SEBON prohibits it by directive
Brokers refuse to execute same-day round trips
The ±3% order band prevents it

questions.explain: It is structural, not regulatory. Shares bought today are credited to your Demat on T+2, and you cannot deliver what is not in your account. No broker can change that, and no directive is needed to prohibit a transaction the system cannot process. Treat anyone offering 'NEPSE intraday' training as a warning sign about everything else they will teach you.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What would you have to deliver, and when does it actually arrive?

questions.stem: A stock moves +1.71% in your favour over a two-day round trip of 500 kitta at Rs. 234. Roughly what do you keep after all costs and tax?

options.t: About +0.87% — roughly half the move
The full +1.71%
About +1.5%
Nothing — costs consume the entire move

questions.explain: Commission on both legs, SEBON fee on both legs, two DP charges and 10% short-term CGT on the gain reduce a +1.71% price move to about +0.87% of net return. Now run it the other way: a −1.71% move produces a loss of about Rs. 2,850 rather than Rs. 1,022, because costs are paid in both directions and there is no tax relief on a loss. Wins are halved and losses are amplified, which is the arithmetic that makes short-horizon trading unattractive here.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Costs are charged on both legs, and the gain is taxed. Roughly what fraction survives?

questions.stem: What is auction settlement?

options.t: NEPSE buys the shares in the market to deliver to the buyer, and charges you the difference plus a penalty
A special session where failed trades are re-matched at the closing price
The buyer's order is cancelled and both parties are made whole
Your broker sells other shares from your portfolio to cover

questions.explain: The buyer is entitled to their shares regardless of what the seller did, so NEPSE buys them in the open market to deliver. Whatever that costs above your sale price is charged to you, plus a penalty, and your broker may restrict your account. Nepal's clearing arrangement guarantees the innocent counterparty — which is precisely why it must charge the failing one, or the guarantee would be funded by people who did nothing wrong.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The buyer must get their shares. Where do those shares come from?

questions.stem: Why is a delivery failure usually worse on a thin counter than on a liquid one?

options.t: Buying the shares in a hurry moves the price against the auction, and you pay that too
Thin counters carry a higher statutory penalty
SEBON charges a liquidity surcharge
The DP charge is higher on thin counters

questions.explain: The auction must buy the shares quickly, and on a counter with little depth that purchase itself pushes the price up. You are charged the difference between your sale price and whatever the auction actually paid — so thin liquidity makes the bill larger in exactly the situation where you can least afford it. The penalty and the DP charge are the same everywhere; it is the market impact that differs.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What happens to the price when someone has to buy 300 kitta immediately on a counter that trades 1,000 a day?

questions.stem: Which of these reduce your risk of a settlement failure? (Select all that apply)

options.t: Authorising EDIS as soon as you see the sale on T+1
Keeping your Demat transaction PIN somewhere you can find quickly
Funding your account before placing a buy order
Placing larger orders so they fill in one day

questions.explain: The first three are the practical defences: act on EDIS early rather than at 14:50, know your PIN, and have cleared funds before you buy. Order size does not affect settlement failure at all — a large order that fills across two days settles twice, but both settlements complete normally provided you authorise each one. Larger orders on a thin counter actually make partial fills MORE likely, not less.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these are about being prepared. One is about order sizing, which is a different problem.

questions.stem: A Rs. 4,90,000 trade costs Rs. 1,617 in commission. A Rs. 5,10,000 trade costs Rs. 1,581. Why does the larger trade cost less?

options.t: Slabs apply to the whole amount, so crossing a boundary re-prices the entire trade at the lower rate
Brokers discount larger trades
The SEBON fee falls above Rs. 5,00,000
It is a rounding artefact in the broker's system

questions.explain: Commission slabs are not marginal. Rs. 4,90,000 sits in the 0.33% slab and pays 0.33% on all of it; Rs. 5,10,000 crosses into the 0.31% slab and pays 0.31% on all of it. The break-even is Rs. 5,00,000 × (0.0033 ÷ 0.0031) = Rs. 5,32,258, so any trade between Rs. 5,00,001 and that figure costs less in commission than a Rs. 5,00,000 trade. The rate is regulated, so no broker discounts it, and the SEBON fee is a flat 0.015% on equity at every size.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Is the slab rate applied only to the amount above the boundary, or to the whole trade?

questions.stem: You buy shares worth exactly Rs. 5,00,000. What is the broker commission, in rupees?
questions.explain: Rs. 5,00,000 falls in the second slab (Rs. 50,001–5,00,000) at 0.33%, and slabs apply to the whole amount, not marginally. 5,00,000 × 0.0033 = Rs. 1,650. One rupee more — Rs. 5,00,001 — moves into the 0.31% slab and costs Rs. 1,550, which is Rs. 100 less. This is a curiosity worth understanding when your contract note arrives, not a reason to size positions around slab boundaries.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Rs. 5,00,000 is the top of the second slab, not the bottom of the third.

questions.stem: You can negotiate a lower commission rate with your broker if you trade frequently.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False. The five slabs are regulated, and the commission is split roughly 79.4% to the broker, 20% to NEPSE and 0.6% to SEBON. Your broker keeps under four fifths of it and cannot discount the regulated portion. If someone offers you a lower rate, be sceptical about everything else they are telling you.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Who actually receives the commission — is it all your broker's to give away?

questions.stem: On a Rs. 1,000 trade, how does the DP charge compare with the commission?

options.t: The DP charge is about seven times the commission
They are roughly equal
The commission is about seven times the DP charge
There is no DP charge on trades under Rs. 5,000

questions.explain: Commission on Rs. 1,000 at 0.36% is Rs. 3.60. The DP charge is a flat Rs. 25 — roughly seven times larger. That ratio inverts completely at scale: on a Rs. 5,00,000 trade the commission is Rs. 1,650 and the DP charge is still Rs. 25, one sixty-sixth of it. The flat charge is what makes very small trades structurally unprofitable, and there is no minimum-size exemption.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Work out 0.36% of Rs. 1,000, then compare it with Rs. 25.

questions.stem: What is the SEBON fee on a Rs. 2,00,000 equity trade, in rupees?
questions.explain: Rs. 2,00,000 × 0.015% = Rs. 30. The SEBON fee is proportional and genuinely small — it never distorts a decision. Note that different instruments carry different rates: 0.015% on equity, 0.010% on corporate debentures, and 0.005% on government and NRB bonds. The charge that actually distorts small trades is the flat Rs. 25 DP charge, not this one.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The equity rate is 0.015%. What is 0.015% of Rs. 2,00,000?

questions.stem: You buy 100 kitta of NABIL in the morning and 150 kitta of NABIL in the afternoon of the same day. What DP charge applies?

options.t: Rs. 25 — one company, one settlement date
Rs. 50 — two separate trades
Rs. 25 per 100 kitta
Nothing until you sell

questions.explain: The DP charge is Rs. 25 per company per settlement date. Both purchases are the same company settling on the same date, so one charge applies. The mirror image is the expensive case: a single order that fills partially across two days settles twice and costs Rs. 50 — which is a real argument for sizing orders you expect to fill completely.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Read the basis precisely: per what, and per what?

questions.stem: You are an individual investor. You bought shares on 1 March 2026 and sold them on 20 February 2027 for a gain of Rs. 40,000. What capital gains tax is withheld?

options.t: Rs. 0 — CGT is paid annually, not withheld

questions.explain: The holding period is 356 days — fewer than 365 — so it is short-term. Since 17 July 2026 the short-term rate for individuals is 10%. Rs. 40,000 × 10% = Rs. 4,000, withheld at source during settlement. Rs. 3,000 would be the 7.5% long-term rate, which needs MORE than 365 days. Rs. 2,000 is the old 5% long-term rate, replaced in July 2026. CGT on listed shares is a final tax withheld at settlement, not filed annually.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Count the days carefully, then check which rate applies after July 2026.

questions.stem: You hold shares for exactly 365 days and sell at a gain. Which rate applies?

options.t: 10% — the short-term rate, because the threshold is MORE than 365 days
7.5% — 365 days qualifies as long-term
5% — the historical long-term rate
It is prorated between the two rates

questions.explain: The long-term threshold is more than 365 days, so exactly 365 is short-term and attracts 10%. Day 366 is the first long-term day. On a Rs. 1,00,000 gain that single day is worth Rs. 2,500 — which is why it is worth knowing the boundary precisely rather than approximately. Rates never prorate; one side of the line or the other applies to the whole gain.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Is the rule '365 or more' or 'more than 365'?

questions.stem: Your MeroShare shows 300 kitta with a WACC of Rs. 412.50. You sell all 300 at Rs. 470.00 after 18 months. Net-of-charges sale proceeds are Rs. 1,40,530. What CGT is withheld?
questions.explain: Cost basis = 300 × 412.50 = Rs. 1,23,750. Gain = 1,40,530 − 1,23,750 = Rs. 16,780. Held 18 months, so long-term: 7.5% since 17 July 2026. 16,780 × 0.075 = Rs. 1,258.50. Rs. 839 applies the old 5% long-term rate replaced in July 2026. Rs. 1,678 applies the 10% short-term rate. Rs. 10,539.75 taxes the gross sale value instead of the gain — a common and expensive misunderstanding.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: CGT is charged on the gain over your cost basis, not on the sale value. And 18 months is which band?

questions.stem: Which of these are true of capital gains tax on listed Nepali shares? (Select all that apply)

options.t: It is withheld at source during settlement
It is a final tax — you do not pay again on that gain
Losses on listed shares generally cannot offset your other income
Bonus shares are taxed when you receive them

questions.explain: CGT is deducted before the money reaches you and is final, so you do not add it to your income and pay again at your slab rate. The flip side of finality is that losses generally cannot be set off against other income — a losing year is simply a losing year. Bonus shares are not a taxable event at issue; they reduce your WACC, so the tax is deferred until you sell, not avoided.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these describe how a final withholding tax behaves. One is about bonus shares.

questions.stem: You buy 10 kitta at Rs. 100. What percentage move do you need just to break even? Answer to two decimals.
questions.explain: 5.77%. Total cost to buy is Rs. 1,028.75 (gross Rs. 1,000, commission Rs. 3.60, SEBON Rs. 0.15, DP Rs. 25), and you pay a second Rs. 25 DP charge plus commission and SEBON on the way out. Break-even is Rs. 105.77. The flat Rs. 25 DP charge alone is 2.5% of a Rs. 1,000 trade — seven times the commission — and you pay it twice. This is why very small trades are structurally unprofitable.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Work out the flat charges first. On Rs. 1,000, what percentage is the DP charge — and how many times do you pay it?

questions.stem: Why does a Rs. 2,30,000 trade need only about a 0.71% move to break even, while a Rs. 1,000 trade needs 5.77%?

options.t: The Rs. 25 DP charge is flat, so it is a much smaller fraction of a large trade
The commission rate is far lower on large trades
Large trades are exempt from the SEBON fee
Capital gains tax is lower on larger positions

questions.explain: The flat DP charge dominates. On Rs. 1,000 it is 2.5% per settlement; on Rs. 2,30,000 it is 0.01%. Commission does fall across slabs but only from 0.36% to 0.33% between these two trades — nowhere near enough to explain an eight-fold difference in the hurdle. There is no SEBON exemption and CGT does not vary with position size. Keep positions at roughly Rs. 25,000 or above to hold round-trip friction under about 1%.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: One of the three charges does not scale with trade size. Which, and what does that do to a small trade?

questions.stem: If you sell below your break-even price, you still owe capital gains tax on the sale.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False. CGT is charged on the gain over your cost basis. Sell below break-even and there is no gain, so no CGT is due — the one small mercy in the arithmetic. Note the flip side, though: you also get no tax relief for the loss, because CGT on listed shares is a final tax and losses generally cannot offset other income.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What is capital gains tax charged on — the sale, or the gain?

questions.stem: Which is the most expensive mistake when computing a round trip by hand?

options.t: Charging CGT on the sale value rather than on the gain
Forgetting the second DP charge
Using the wrong commission slab
Applying the SEBON fee to only one leg

questions.explain: Taxing the sale value instead of the gain overstates the tax roughly ninefold on a typical trade — Rs. 11,200 instead of Rs. 1,200 on a Rs. 1,12,000 sale with a Rs. 12,000 gain. The other three are real errors but small: a missed DP charge is Rs. 25, a wrong slab is tens of rupees, and a missed SEBON leg is a few rupees. Get the tax base right first.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Compare the size of each error in rupees on a Rs. 1,12,000 sale.

questions.stem: You buy 300 kitta at Rs. 330.00. What is the total cost including commission, SEBON fee and DP charge, in rupees?
questions.explain: Gross = 300 × 330 = Rs. 99,000. That sits in the 0.33% slab, so commission = Rs. 326.70. SEBON fee at 0.015% = Rs. 14.85. DP charge = Rs. 25. Total = Rs. 99,366.55, giving a WACC of Rs. 331.22 per share. That WACC — not Rs. 330 — is your cost basis for capital gains tax, and it is the figure MeroShare will show you.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Gross, then commission at the slab rate, then 0.015%, then the flat Rs. 25.

questions.stem: How many DP charges does a complete round trip — one buy and one sell, each settling on a single date — incur?
questions.explain: Two: one on the buy settlement and one on the sell settlement, at Rs. 25 each. A round trip always carries at least two. If either leg fills partially across two days it settles twice, adding another Rs. 25 — which is why an order sized to fill completely is worth a moment's thought before you place it.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: How many settlements happen in a buy-then-sell round trip?

questions.stem: Which section of an IPO prospectus tells you what the company will actually do with your money?

options.t: Objectives of the Issue
Risk Factors
Capital Structure
Auditor's Report

questions.explain: Objectives of the Issue states the intended use of proceeds, and the difference between 'construction of the powerhouse and transmission line' and 'repayment of promoter loans and working capital' is the difference between funding an asset and funding someone's exit. The other sections are all worth reading, but only this one answers what your rupees will build. Every SEBON-approved prospectus is published at sebon.gov.np.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The section name says exactly what it contains.

questions.stem: When you buy shares of a listed company on NEPSE, the company receives your money.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False. That is a secondary-market trade — your money goes to the investor who sold to you, and the company is not a party to it. Money reaches a company only through the primary market: an IPO, FPO or rights issue. This is why the phrase 'the company gained Rs. 50 crore in market value today' describes an opinion changing, not a rupee entering the business.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Did the company create these shares today, or did they already exist in someone's Demat?

questions.stem: Under C-ASBA, what happens to your application money while the issue is open?

options.t: It is blocked in your own bank account and debited only if you are allotted
It is transferred to the issuer and refunded if you are not allotted
It is held in escrow by CDSC
It is transferred to your broker's collection account

questions.explain: C-ASBA means Centralised Application Supported by Blocked Amount. The money stays in your account, earning whatever interest your account pays, and is debited only if shares are actually allotted. If you are not allotted, the block simply lifts — no refund to chase, no float lost, no counterparty risk. It is the best-designed part of the Nepali market, and it is why any request to transfer IPO money anywhere is a scam.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What does the 'BA' in ASBA stand for?

questions.stem: You submit a second application for the same issue through a different bank, hoping to double your odds. What happens?

options.t: Both applications may be voided — one per person per issue
Your odds double, since each application enters the lottery
The second is ignored and the first stands
Both are accepted but only one can be allotted

questions.explain: The rule is one application per person per issue — not per bank account, not per Demat. Duplicates are rejected and submitting a second can void both, leaving you with nothing when you would otherwise have had a valid entry. People do this believing it improves their odds; it does the opposite. Applying through a family member's Demat is that person's application, with their own odds and their own shares.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Is the limit per application, per bank account, or per person?

questions.stem: What is the retail minimum in a book-built issue, and why does it matter?

options.t: 50 units — roughly five times the fixed-price minimum, a real barrier for small applicants
10 units, the same as a fixed-price issue
100 units, the same as a mutual fund
There is no minimum in book building

questions.explain: The book-building retail minimum is 50 units against 10 for a fixed-price issue. At any realistic discovered price that is several thousand rupees rather than Rs. 1,000, which meaningfully raises the entry cost for retail — for the same single lottery ticket, since odds are equal per valid application either way. Retail does receive a 10% discount to the institutional price, but that is a discount to what institutions bid, not to what the business is worth.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Fixed price is 10 units. Book building is five times that.

questions.stem: A company wants to issue shares above the Rs. 100 face value. What must it satisfy?

options.t: Rs. 1 arba paid-up capital and two consecutive profitable years
Any company may price above face value if SEBON approves the prospectus
Three consecutive profitable years and a NEPSE listing
A credit rating of at least investment grade

questions.explain: Premium pricing eligibility requires Rs. 1 arba of paid-up capital and two consecutive profitable years. It is a real bar, not a formality — it exists to stop unproven companies charging a premium on the strength of a story. Companies that do not meet it issue at the Rs. 100 face value, which is why most small hydropower IPOs are fixed-price at par.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Two conditions: one about size, one about profitability.

questions.stem: A fixed-price IPO offers 1,00,000 units. 5,00,000 valid applications are received, all for the 10-unit minimum. You applied for 100 units instead of 10. Your chance of allotment is:

options.t: The same as everyone else's
Ten times higher
Zero, since the maximum is 10
Guaranteed, since you applied for more

questions.explain: Nepali fixed-price allotment runs a computerised lottery in which each valid application has equal probability regardless of size. In a heavily oversubscribed issue, allotment is typically the minimum lot to as many applicants as possible — so if you win, you receive 10 units, the same as everyone else. Applying for more units simply ties up ten times the money in ASBA blocking for identical odds and an identical outcome.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Does the lottery draw applications, or units?

questions.stem: An issue offers 2,00,000 units with a 10-unit minimum lot. 4,00,000 valid applications arrive. What is your approximate chance of allotment, as a percentage?
questions.explain: 2,00,000 units ÷ 10 units per allottee = 20,000 applicants can be allotted. 20,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = 5%. The general form is (units on offer ÷ minimum lot) ÷ number of valid applications. In popular Nepali issues this typically lands between 5% and 25%. The expected value is attractive because an unsuccessful application costs nothing but the opportunity cost of the blocked funds.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: First work out how many people can be allotted, then divide by the number applying.

questions.stem: You hold 100 shares at Rs. 600. A 1:2 rights issue at Rs. 400 is announced and you do nothing. What happens to your position?

options.t: You still hold 100 shares, but the price adjusts to about Rs. 533 — you lose roughly Rs. 6,667 of value
Nothing changes — you simply do not participate
The rights are sold on your behalf and the proceeds credited
You are allotted the shares anyway and billed later

questions.explain: Unexercised rights lapse. The price still adjusts to roughly the theoretical ex-rights level of Rs. 533.33 because everyone else's shares were issued, and you still hold 100. 100 × 533.33 = Rs. 53,333 against the Rs. 60,000 you started with — about Rs. 6,667 destroyed by inaction, with nothing on any statement to tell you. Some rights are renounceable and can be sold; if yours are not, the value is simply forfeited.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The price adjusts whether or not you participate. What does that do to someone who did not?

questions.stem: Which corporate action actually puts cash in your pocket?

options.t: A cash dividend, net of 5% tax at source
A bonus issue
A stock split
A rights issue

questions.explain: Only a cash dividend pays you money, and individuals receive it net of 5% deducted at source. A bonus issue gives you more shares of the same total value and lowers your WACC, deferring tax rather than avoiding it. A split is cosmetic — the face value divides and the price divides with it. A rights issue takes money FROM you; it is a capital call at a discount, and exercising it leaves you exactly level.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these change your share count. Only one moves cash.

questions.stem: You hold 100 shares with a WACC of Rs. 600 and receive a 20% bonus. What is your new WACC, in rupees?
questions.explain: Your total cost is unchanged at Rs. 60,000, and a 20% bonus gives you 120 shares. 60,000 ÷ 120 = Rs. 500. You are not richer — the market price adjusts down on the ex-bonus date by roughly the same proportion. What has changed is your future tax: when you sell, the gain is computed against Rs. 500 rather than Rs. 600, so the tax not paid at issue arrives later, in full. Bonus shares defer tax; they do not avoid it.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Total cost stays the same. Only the number of shares it is spread across changes.

questions.stem: Why do Nepali closed-end funds persistently trade below their NAV? (Select all that apply)

options.t: You cannot redeem units for NAV — your only exit is selling to another investor
Management fees accrue against the assets every year
Fund units are thinly traded, so the spread and exit difficulty push the price down
SEBON caps the market price of fund units below NAV

questions.explain: The first three are the real reasons: no redemption right, ongoing fees between you and the NAV, and thin liquidity. There is no regulatory cap on the price — the discount is a market outcome, not a rule. Maturity is what forces convergence, since a closed-end fund liquidates and distributes NAV at the end of its fixed term, which is why years-to-maturity matters as much as the size of the discount.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these are structural features of a closed-end fund. One invents a rule that does not exist.

questions.stem: Two funds both trade at Rs. 9.20 against an NAV of Rs. 11.40. One matures in two years, the other in eight. Both charge 1.5% a year. Which is the better proposition, and why?

options.t: The two-year fund — the same discount closes sooner, with about 3% lost to fees instead of 12%
The eight-year fund — more time for the underlying portfolio to grow
They are identical, since the discount is the same
The eight-year fund — longer funds trade at wider discounts, so it will re-rate

questions.explain: Maturity forces the discount to zero, so the catalyst is dated. The two-year fund reaches it after roughly 3% of NAV has gone in fees; the eight-year fund after roughly 12% — most of the discount you were buying. The identical headline discount conceals very different propositions. And in both cases the discount is a cushion, not a floor: NAV itself can fall, as it did roughly 50% across the 2021–2023 drawdown.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: How much of the NAV disappears in fees before the maturity catalyst arrives in each case?

questions.stem: What is the face value of a Nepali mutual fund unit, in rupees?
questions.explain: Rs. 10, not Rs. 100 — mutual fund units use a different convention from ordinary shares. The minimum application is 100 units, so Rs. 1,000, the same entry cost as a fixed-price share IPO. Do not read a fund's Rs. 8.40 price as 'cheap' any more than you would read a bank trading below Rs. 100; the number to compare against is NAV, not face value.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Ordinary shares are Rs. 100. Mutual fund units are one tenth of that.

questions.stem: A candle has a small body sitting at the top of its range, with a long lower wick. What does that describe?

options.t: Sellers pushed price down hard and buyers absorbed all of it before the close
Buyers pushed price up and could not hold the gains
Almost no trading took place
The session opened and closed at the same price with no movement

questions.explain: The lower wick is ground that was taken and given back: sellers drove price down, buyers bought all of it, and the close finished near the high. That is strength. The mirror image — a small body at the bottom of a long upper wick — is weakness, where buyers ran price up and could not hold it. Note that this reading is incomplete on its own: whether it matters depends entirely on what came before, which is Lesson 9.5.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The wick is ground taken and then given back. Which side took it, and who won it back?

questions.stem: A stock closes exactly 15% above its previous close, with a long body and no upper wick. What is the honest reading?

options.t: It hit the circuit limit — price stopped because it was not allowed to move further
A bullish marubozu — buyers controlled every minute of the session
A bearish reversal, because there is no upper wick
A data error, since 15% moves are not possible

questions.explain: ±15% of the previous close is the daily circuit limit, raised from ±10% on 21 April 2026. A close sitting exactly on it means trading stopped moving the price, not that buyers and sellers reached agreement. The shape mimics a marubozu but means something different: demand that was queued behind the limit is invisible and is usually still there tomorrow. Check the arithmetic before reading the shape.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What is 15% of the previous close, and what rule sits exactly there?

questions.stem: What distinguishes a hammer from a hanging man?

options.t: Nothing in the drawing — only the trend that preceded it
The hammer has a longer lower wick
The hanging man has no upper wick at all
The hammer is hollow and the hanging man is filled

questions.explain: They are drawn identically: small body at the top, long lower wick, minimal upper wick. A hammer follows a decline and is bullish; a hanging man follows an advance and is bearish. The candle describes the same event — sellers pushed, buyers absorbed — but the population of people it describes is completely different. This is why the detectors in this course compute the preceding trend before naming anything.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Try drawing both. What is different about the picture?

questions.stem: What does a doji record?

options.t: Indecision — the session settled essentially nothing
A guaranteed reversal
That the stock hit its circuit limit
Heavy institutional buying

questions.explain: A doji has essentially no body: open and close are the same, so nothing was settled however far price travelled intraday. It is not a reversal signal on its own — it records indecision, and indecision means something only after an extended trend. A doji in the middle of a sideways drift is exactly what a sideways drift looks like.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The body is the settled result. What does it mean when there is essentially no body?

questions.stem: In a bullish engulfing pattern, the second candle's wicks must completely engulf the first candle's wicks.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False — only the bodies need to be engulfed. Beginners reject perfectly valid signals over this constantly. The pattern says sentiment reversed inside a single session and buyers overwhelmed the prior day's settled result; the wicks are ground taken and given back, and are not part of the test.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which part of a candle is the settled result — the body or the wicks?

questions.stem: A textbook bullish engulfing appears on a counter whose two candles traded 410 and 180 kitta, on a 20-day average turnover of Rs. 1.9 lakh. What should you do?

options.t: Nothing — the pattern is geometrically real but describes two people, not a crowd
Buy, since the pattern is valid by every test
Buy a smaller position to reduce the risk
Wait for a second engulfing pattern to confirm

questions.explain: A pattern is a statement about what a crowd did. 180 kitta at around Rs. 168 is roughly Rs. 30,000 of trading — one order. The geometry passed and the information did not. Sizing down does not help, because the problem is that the signal is meaningless, not that the position is large; and a second meaningless pattern is not confirmation. With 141 of 271 listed companies in hydropower and microfinance, much of NEPSE is thin enough for this to matter constantly.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: How many separate decisions does 180 kitta of trading represent?

questions.stem: A morning star's third candle closes at Rs. 303.10. Candle one ran from Rs. 318.00 down to Rs. 296.00. Does the pattern qualify?

options.t: No — it must close above candle one's midpoint of Rs. 307.00
Yes — it closed above candle one's low
Yes — three candles in that sequence always qualify
No — it must close above candle one's open of Rs. 318.00

questions.explain: The midpoint of candle one is (318 + 296) ÷ 2 = Rs. 307.00, and the third candle must close above it. At Rs. 303.10 it did not, so buyers took back less than half the damage — that is a bounce, not a handover of control. Requiring a close above the full open would be far too strict and almost no morning star would qualify. Rules like this are arithmetic precisely so patterns do not become a matter of squinting.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Work out the midpoint of the first candle's body, then compare.

questions.stem: Three white soldiers have printed. What does the pattern tell you?

options.t: The trend has genuine participation — it confirms rather than triggers
A reversal is beginning
The stock is overbought and should be sold
Volume has collapsed

questions.explain: Three consecutive strong bullish candles, each opening inside the previous body and closing above the previous close, confirm that a trend has real participation. It is not a reversal signal. The practical warning is that by the time three soldiers have printed, a good deal of the move has already happened — treat it as confirmation of a trend you had already identified from structure, not as an entry trigger.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Is this pattern describing a change of direction, or the continuation of one?

questions.stem: Three charts show an identical hammer candle. In which is it a meaningful bullish signal?

options.t: After a five-day decline into a level that has held twice before, on above-average volume
In the middle of a two-week sideways drift, on average volume
After a three-week advance to a new high
All three equally — the candle is identical

questions.explain: The first has both ingredients: a decline that trapped sellers, and a level where buyers were waiting, with volume confirming. In the second the same candle sits mid-range in a drift — nobody was trapped, so nobody has to buy back, and it is noise. In the third it appears after an advance, which makes it a hanging man and bearish, despite being drawn identically. A candle's shape is half its meaning; everything before it is the other half.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Ask two questions of each: why were sellers pushing, and why would buyers be waiting there?

questions.stem: Why is waiting for confirmation before acting on a candlestick pattern especially worthwhile on NEPSE?

options.t: Because round-trip friction is about 1% and illiquid positions cannot be exited quickly, so being wrong is expensive
Because NEPSE requires a confirmation candle before an order can be placed
Because confirmation raises the accuracy of the pattern to nearly 100%
Because capital gains tax is lower on confirmed trades
