questions.explain: Confirmation costs you part of the move and removes a large share of false signals. That trade-off is worth making wherever being wrong is expensive — and on NEPSE it is, because every round trip costs roughly 1% in commission, SEBON fee and two DP charges, and a thin counter may take days to exit. There is no exchange rule about confirmation, no accuracy guarantee, and tax does not vary by how you entered.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What does being wrong actually cost you on this market, compared with being late?

questions.stem: A chart shows a stock 'crashing 17% overnight' three years ago. Before drawing any conclusion, what should you check?

options.t: Whether that was an ex-bonus date and the chart is unadjusted
Whether the exchange was closed that day
Whether the stock hit its circuit limit
Whether the SEBON fee changed that year

questions.explain: On an ex-bonus date the price adjusts down mechanically by the bonus proportion — nothing happened to the business. Nepali banks and microfinance companies issue bonus shares frequently, so these gaps are common. If the chart is unadjusted, every level drawn across that date connects prices that are not on the same scale. A 17% overnight fall could not be a circuit day anyway, since the limit is 15%.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What corporate action makes a price drop overnight without anything happening to the company?

questions.stem: Which checks should you run before trusting any candlestick pattern on NEPSE? (Select all that apply)

options.t: Is the close sitting exactly at ±15% of the previous close?
Does the chart span an unadjusted bonus or rights date?
What is the 20-day average turnover?
Is the pattern listed in the top ten most reliable patterns?

questions.explain: The three checks are circuit, corporate actions and turnover — they take under a minute together and eliminate most false signals. Reliability rankings are a rough guide at best and do nothing about the three ways NEPSE specifically breaks pattern analysis: prices stopped by the limit rather than discovered, mechanical gaps on corporate-action dates, and counters too thin for a pattern to describe a crowd at all.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these are about whether the data is trustworthy. One is about the pattern's reputation.

questions.stem: How is an uptrend defined?

options.t: Higher highs and higher lows
Price above the 50-day moving average
More green candles than red over the last month
RSI above 50

questions.explain: An uptrend is higher highs AND higher lows; a downtrend is lower highs and lower lows; anything else is a range. The definition uses swing points only, so it needs no indicator and produces no argument. The other three options are all functions of price computed after the fact — useful as descriptions, but they lag the structure they are derived from.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The definition uses only the peaks and troughs the price itself makes.

questions.stem: A stock in an uptrend makes a lower high but its last swing low still holds. What is the status?

options.t: A warning — the uptrend is intact until a lower low prints
The uptrend has broken
A downtrend has begun
Nothing has changed at all

questions.explain: An uptrend needs both higher highs and higher lows. A lower high removes one leg, which is worth noticing, but the trend breaks only on a lower low — the first time buyers fail to defend a level they previously defended. This distinction keeps people in good positions: selling on a lower high means selling into a pause and paying about 1% round-trip for it, while waiting for the lower low gives an unambiguous exit that does not depend on how the chart feels.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Two conditions define an uptrend. How many have failed here?

questions.stem: Line A has four touches and no violations. Line B has one touch and two violations. Which is a real level?

options.t: Line A — repeated touches with no clean break is evidence
Line B — recent price action matters more than old touches
Both, at different timeframes
Neither — support and resistance are not real

questions.explain: Two touches make a level and three or more make one worth respecting; one touch is just a low. Line B has been passed straight through twice, which is direct evidence against it. This test is countable, which is what separates drawing levels from wishing — and the honest caveat is that Line A will break eventually too. Its value is that it gives you a defined place to be wrong, which Lesson 14.2 turns into a position size.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Count the touches, then count the times price went straight through.

questions.stem: Why should you treat a support level as a zone rather than a precise price?

options.t: Markets are made of people, who do not act to the paisa — a precise level produces stops hit by noise
NEPSE rounds all prices to the nearest rupee
Because the ±3% order band prevents precise entries
Because levels are only valid on weekly charts

questions.explain: A level of 'Rs. 232' is really Rs. 230–234. Treating it as an exact number produces stops that ordinary noise takes out, costing you about 1% round-trip each time for nothing. NEPSE quotes to the paisa, not the rupee; the ±3% band restricts how far from the LTP you may place an order but not the precision of the price; and levels work on any timeframe.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What is a level actually made of — a rule, or thousands of individual decisions?

questions.stem: What most raises the odds that a breakout is genuine rather than a fakeout?

options.t: A close beyond the level on above-average volume
An intraday touch beyond the level
A large gap on the opening print
RSI above 70 at the moment of the break

questions.explain: Volume tells you how many participants agreed, and the close — not the intraday touch — tells you the break held. Price poking through and closing back inside is a wick, not a breakout. A gap says nothing on its own and on NEPSE may be a corporate-action adjustment. RSI above 70 simply reflects that the move has been one-sided, which is what a breakout looks like anyway.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Two things matter: how many people agreed, and whether it held to the close.

questions.stem: Entering on the retest rather than the break costs you some upside. Why is that trade usually right on NEPSE?

options.t: Because being wrong is expensive here — 1% friction, no stop-loss order type, and thin counters you cannot exit
Because retests are more accurate about direction
Because NEPSE charges lower commission on retest entries
Because a retest guarantees the level has flipped permanently

questions.explain: The retest rule does not make you more accurate about direction — it makes your losses less frequent, which is a different and more durable advantage. That matters most where being wrong is costly: roughly 1% round-trip friction, no automatic stop-loss on NEPSE, and counters that may take days to exit. Commission does not vary by entry style, and nothing about a retest is a guarantee.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Compare the cost of being wrong on this market against the cost of being late.

questions.stem: A thin counter shows a breakout on volume 4× its average — the strongest relative volume of any candidate you have found. Its 20-day average turnover is Rs. 2 lakh. You want a Rs. 2,00,000 position. What is the problem?

options.t: Your position is an entire normal day's turnover — you would be the breakout, and you could not exit
There is no problem — 4× volume is exactly the confirmation you wanted
The commission would be too high at that size
The ±15% circuit would prevent the order

questions.explain: Relative volume looks convincing and absolute turnover is negligible. A Rs. 2,00,000 position equals 100% of a normal day, so your own buying is the move, and exiting takes roughly ten trading days at 10% of turnover — during which your selling pushes the price down. Commission is proportional and unremarkable; the circuit limits daily price movement, not order size. Read absolute turnover in rupees, not the height of the volume bar.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Compare your intended position with one day's total turnover in rupees.

questions.stem: A counter averages Rs. 20 lakh of daily turnover. Assuming you can be at most 10% of a day's volume, what is the largest position you could exit in two trading days, in rupees?
questions.explain: 10% of Rs. 20 lakh is Rs. 2,00,000 sellable per day; over two days that is Rs. 4,00,000. Beyond that you are either taking longer to exit or becoming a large enough share of the volume that you move the price against yourself. This calculation is part of position sizing, not separate from it — a position you cannot leave in about two days is one whose risk you do not control, and NEPSE offers no stop-loss order type to help.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Work out how much you can sell in one day, then double it.

questions.stem: The order book shows 18,400 kitta offered at Rs. 300 and about 1,500 at every neighbouring price. Where should you place your own sell order?

options.t: Just below Rs. 300 — at Rs. 300 you queue behind 18,400 kitta
Exactly at Rs. 300, to get the round number
Well above Rs. 300, since the wall will break
It makes no difference — allocation is proportional

questions.explain: Matching is by price then time, so an order at Rs. 300 sits behind 18,400 kitta already queued there. Placing at Rs. 299.50 fills ahead of all of them; on a 500-share position the fifty paisa costs Rs. 250, which is usually far less than the queue position is worth. Allocation is never proportional on NEPSE — the earliest order at a price fills completely before the next one gets anything.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Matching is by price, then by time. What happens to an order joining the back of a very long queue?

questions.stem: How many touches should a trendline have before it is worth drawing?
questions.explain: Three. Two points define any line at all, so two touches prove nothing — you can draw a line through any two points on any chart. The common failure is drawing the line first and hunting for touches afterwards. Mark the swing points, then see whether a line fits; if you have to ignore a swing to make it work, it does not work.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: How many points does it take to define a line? You need more than that.

questions.stem: The Rs. 100 face value acts as a psychological level on NEPSE even though it carries no information about value.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: True, and it is the strongest anchor in the Nepali market because it is printed on the instrument itself. Face value is an accounting convention used for paid-up capital and IPO pricing — Lesson 1.4 took that apart. But holders who bought at issue treat Rs. 100 as 'getting my money back', so selling often accelerates as a struggling counter approaches it from above. The accounts do not change at Rs. 100; the order book does.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Does something have to be economically meaningful to affect how people behave?

questions.stem: What is a moving average genuinely good at?

options.t: Describing the regime — whether price is above or below a rising or falling average
Timing entries precisely
Predicting where price will turn
Working reliably in ranging markets

questions.explain: A moving average is an average of the past and lags by construction, so it cannot time entries or predict turns. What it does well is summarise the regime: above a rising 200-day is a different world from below a falling one, and that single reading is worth more than every crossover signal combined. In ranges it is at its worst, sitting in the middle and crossing back and forth — and most charts are ranging most of the time.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: It is an average of prices that already happened. What can that possibly do well?

questions.stem: Why is an SMA 200 unreliable on a Nepali counter that listed eighteen months ago and has gone ex-bonus twice?

options.t: It is computed over a series that is partly mechanical adjustment and partly halted trading
SMA 200 only works on indices, not individual shares
NEPSE does not publish 200 sessions of history for new listings
Bonus shares increase the share count, which invalidates all averages

questions.explain: The 200-day average needs 200 sessions of clean, comparable data. On a recently listed counter with two ex-bonus adjustments and circuit days scattered through it, a large part of the window is either a mechanical price adjustment or a session where the price was stopped rather than discovered. NEPSE does publish the history; the problem is what that history contains. Check the chart is bonus-adjusted before reading any long average.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What has to be true about the 200 prices being averaged for the average to mean anything?

questions.stem: RSI has been above 70 for three weeks. What does that tell you?

options.t: Recent up-sessions have been much larger than down-sessions — which is what a strong trend looks like
The stock is expensive and should be sold
A reversal is imminent
The stock has hit its circuit limit repeatedly

questions.explain: RSI compares the size of recent gains with recent losses. A high reading means the movement has been one-sided, which is precisely what a genuine uptrend produces — so selling because RSI is 74 means selling because the trend is strong. Overbought can stay overbought for months. RSI says nothing about whether the price is high relative to earnings, book value or anything real.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: RSI measures the character of recent movement. Does it know anything about the company?

questions.stem: Price makes a higher high but RSI makes a lower high. What is that, and what should you do?

options.t: Bearish divergence — a reason to tighten a stop or stop adding, not to reverse
Bearish divergence — sell immediately and short the stock
A bullish signal, since price is still making higher highs
A calculation error — RSI must follow price

questions.explain: That is bearish divergence: the new price high was achieved with less momentum than the last one, which is a genuine deterioration in the character of the move. It is a warning, not a reversal signal — divergences persist and fail regularly. And on NEPSE you could not short it in any case, since there is no short selling. Treat it as a reason to tighten a stop or stop adding.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Price and momentum are disagreeing. Is that proof of a reversal, or a warning about its character?

questions.stem: What does the MACD histogram actually measure?

options.t: The gap between momentum and its own average — the rate at which momentum is changing
Total traded volume for the session
The difference between the current price and the 26-day EMA
Whether the stock is overbought or oversold

questions.explain: The MACD line is EMA(12) − EMA(26), which is momentum. The signal line is a 9-period EMA of that. The histogram is the gap between them — the rate at which momentum itself is changing. That is why a shrinking histogram above zero warns of deceleration well before any crossover: the trend is still positive and losing steam. Volume is not an input to MACD at all.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The MACD line is momentum. The histogram is the gap between momentum and what?

questions.stem: A MACD value of 4.2 means the same thing on Everest Bank at Rs. 670 as on a counter trading at Rs. 89.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False. MACD is a rupee difference between two moving averages, so it has no absolute scale — 4.2 rupees of gap is a much larger signal on a Rs. 89 share than on a Rs. 670 one. Compare MACD only against its own history for the same stock, never across stocks, and treat any MACD figure quoted in a group chat without its context as meaningless.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What are the units of the MACD line?

questions.stem: Which features of NEPSE break the assumptions indicators rely on? (Select all that apply)

options.t: Stale closes on counters where almost nothing traded
Circuit-limit closes, where the price was stopped rather than discovered
Unadjusted gaps on ex-bonus and ex-rights dates
The 11:00–15:00 trading session being shorter than other markets

questions.explain: Indicators assume a fair, continuously discovered closing price. Stale closes, circuit-limited closes and mechanical corporate-action gaps all violate that in different ways. The length of the session does not — a four-hour session still produces a genuine close on a liquid counter. The danger is that an indicator never reports an error: it draws a smooth, confident curve from whatever it is given.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these corrupt the closing price itself. One is just a shorter day.

questions.stem: A thin counter shows RSI 78, a large positive MACD histogram, and price above its SMA 50. Six of the last twenty sessions had no trading and three closed at the circuit limit. What are the indicators measuring?

options.t: Three limit-up closes and six days of nothing
Genuine, powerful buying pressure
Institutional accumulation
An imminent reversal, since all three are extended

questions.explain: Every one of those indicators is a function of the closing price, and here the closing prices are mostly limit closes and days with no trading. The readings look stronger than the liquid bank's precisely because they are computed from almost nothing. Worse, this is the counter you would need about ten trading days to exit at a 2.8% spread — the least reliable signal sits on the hardest position to leave.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Look at the input data, not the output numbers. What are those twenty closes actually made of?

questions.stem: Why is adding a third correlated momentum indicator usually worse than useless?

options.t: It manufactures confidence — one piece of evidence triple-counted leads to larger positions on weaker reasoning
It slows down the charting software
Indicators cancel each other out mathematically
SEBON limits the number of indicators a retail investor may use

questions.explain: Most indicators are computed from the same closing prices, so most are highly correlated. Three of them agreeing feels like strong evidence and is really one piece of evidence stated three times — which leads to larger positions on weaker reasoning, exactly backwards. The second failure is paralysis: with six indicators some always disagree, so you either wait for alignment that never comes or pick whichever subset supports the trade you already wanted.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: If three indicators use the same input data, how many independent opinions do you have?

questions.stem: What single filter improves a NEPSE system more than any additional indicator?

options.t: A minimum 20-day average turnover
A longer moving average
A stricter RSI threshold
Requiring three indicators to agree

questions.explain: A liquidity filter removes more bad trades than any indicator adds, because it eliminates the counters where patterns are meaningless, spreads are wide and exits take days. It is not an indicator at all. The other three options all tighten a signal computed from price, which does nothing about the underlying problem: with 141 of 271 listed companies in hydropower and microfinance, much of the exchange is not tradeable at retail size with a stop.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The most valuable filter is not computed from price at all.

questions.stem: System A wins 50% of trades with an average win of 2.1R against an average loss of 1.0R. System B wins 67% but its average win is only 0.7R against the same 1.0R loss. Which has the better expectancy?

options.t: System A — +0.55R per trade against System B's +0.14R
System B — the higher win rate wins
They are identical
It cannot be determined without knowing the position sizes

questions.explain: Expectancy = (win rate x average win) - (loss rate x average loss). System A: (0.50 x 2.1) - (0.50 x 1.0) = +0.55R. System B: (0.67 x 0.7) - (0.33 x 1.0) = +0.14R. System B is right twice as often and makes a quarter as much per trade, because it takes profits early and lets losses run the full stop — the loss-aversion profile from Lesson 15.2. R-multiples make the two comparable regardless of position size.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Multiply the win rate by the average win, then subtract the loss rate times the average loss. Do it for both.

questions.stem: Where is the authoritative source for a Nepali listed company's quarterly numbers?

options.t: The company's own website, under Unaudited Financial Results
Sharesansar's comparison tables
Merolagani's company page
A NEPSE broker's research note

questions.explain: The company publishes its own unaudited quarterly results, and everything else is a copy. Sharesansar, Merolagani and NepseAlpha are genuinely useful for screening and history, but they can be stale, they can transcribe wrongly, and they verify nothing. Use them to find candidates and open the company's own PDF before committing money — it takes five minutes and almost nobody does it, which is the entire edge available to a careful retail investor.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Who actually produces the numbers in the first place?

questions.stem: An aggregator shows EPS of Rs. 34.12 as 'annualised Q1'. Why is that likely to flatter?

options.t: Q4 carries most of a bank's provisioning, so multiplying Q1 by four systematically overstates the year
Annualising always understates earnings
Q1 is the weakest quarter for Nepali banks
Annualised figures exclude interest income

questions.explain: Nepali fiscal quarters begin in Shrawan, and most of a bank's loan-loss provisioning lands in Q4. Multiplying Q1 profit by four therefore projects a year without the provisioning that will actually arrive, so it overstates. Use trailing twelve months where you can. The difference is not trivial: it can move a P/E from 16.71× to 18.40× — the difference between looking cheaper than the sector median of 14.92× and looking above it.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which quarter carries the year's provisioning, and is it included when you multiply Q1 by four?

questions.stem: A company reported EPS of Rs. 36.00 last year, then issued a 20% bonus. To compare fairly with this year's reported EPS, what is last year's adjusted EPS, in rupees?
questions.explain: Adjusted EPS = 36.00 ÷ (1 + 0.20) = Rs. 30.00. The share count grew 20%, so historical per-share figures must be divided by 1.20 to sit on the same scale. Without this adjustment a company growing profits 20% a year can appear to have flat or falling earnings — and a screener sorting on EPS growth would rank it near the bottom. Apply the same divisor to prior prices before drawing any level across the bonus date.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Divide by (1 + the bonus ratio).

questions.stem: Receiving bonus shares avoids capital gains tax on the value they represent.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False — it defers the tax, it does not avoid it. Bonus shares are not a taxable event when received, but they reduce your WACC across the whole holding. Buy 100 kitta at Rs. 600 and receive a 20% bonus, and you hold 120 kitta at a WACC of Rs. 500. When you eventually sell, the gain is computed against Rs. 500 rather than Rs. 600 — so the tax not paid at issue arrives later, in full.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What happens to your cost basis when the share count rises but the total cost does not?

questions.stem: What was the median P/E of Nepali commercial banks in Q2 FY 2082/83?
questions.explain: 14.92× is the sector median and the reference point you should compare against, rather than a remembered figure from another market. 7.67× was the lowest (NBL, with an ROE of just 6.76% — cheap because it earns poorly) and 343.16× the highest (NICA, whose EPS collapsed to Rs. 1.76). The range itself is the lesson: P/E used carelessly in Nepali banking tells you almost nothing.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The median sits between the 7.67× low and the 343.16× high — and it is close to the middle of the pack.

questions.stem: Laxmi Sunrise reported EPS of −Rs. 2.04. What should you do with its P/E?

options.t: Ignore it entirely — P/E is arithmetically meaningless when EPS is negative
Treat it as very cheap
Treat it as very expensive
Use the absolute value of EPS

questions.explain: Dividing a positive price by a negative EPS produces a number with no useful interpretation. Ignore it and look instead at P/B, at why earnings are negative, and at whether the loss is one-off or structural. Taking the absolute value would be inventing data. This is one of the specific cases where a screener sorting on P/E will rank a company nonsensically.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What does price divided by a negative number actually tell you?

questions.stem: Bank X has ROA 1.40% and leverage 10×. Bank Y has ROA 0.70% and leverage 20×. Both show ROE of 14%. What is the difference?

options.t: Bank Y produces the same ROE from leverage, so a 1% loan-book loss hurts it roughly twice as much
There is no difference — identical ROE means identical quality
Bank Y is better, because it uses capital more efficiently
Bank X is riskier, because higher ROA means riskier lending

questions.explain: ROE = ROA × leverage, so 1.40% × 10 and 0.70% × 20 both give 14%. But a 1% loss on the loan book takes Bank X's ROE to roughly 4% and Bank Y's to roughly −6%, because Y has half the equity cushion per rupee of assets. Identical headline number, very different fragility — and the ROE column alone will never show it. This is why NRB sets capital adequacy requirements, which cap the leverage term.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Work out what a 1% loss on assets does to each bank's equity.

questions.stem: What does net interest margin measure, and why did it compress across Nepali banks in 2021–2023?

options.t: The spread between lending and deposit rates — it compressed because NRB tightened and deposit competition raised funding costs
The bank's profit margin after tax — it fell because corporate tax rose
The proportion of loans that are non-performing — it rose as borrowers defaulted
The gap between book value and market price — it narrowed as prices fell

questions.explain: NIM is the spread a bank earns between what it charges borrowers and pays depositors, as a percentage of earning assets — the core engine of a commercial bank. Through 2021–2023 NRB tightened, the system-wide credit-to-deposit ratio was already stretched, and fixed deposit rates rose above 11%. Funding got more expensive for every bank at once, which is why earnings fell across the sector rather than at one bank.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: A bank borrows from depositors and lends to borrowers. What is the margin between those two?

questions.stem: Why does rising NPL predict a bank's future EPS better than its current P/E?

options.t: Bad loans require provisions, provisions reduce profit, and that chain takes two to four quarters to reach EPS
NPL is audited while EPS is not
P/E is not published quarterly
NPL directly determines the share price

questions.explain: P/E tells you what the market thinks about earnings already reported. NPL tells you about earnings not yet reported: loans go bad, the bank provisions against them, provisions reduce profit, and profit reduces EPS — a chain that takes two to four quarters to complete. The first link is published quarterly, on page one, and appears on almost no price-tracking site. That gap is the informational edge available to a careful retail investor.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Trace the sequence from a loan going bad to EPS falling. How long does it take?

questions.stem: A bank's credit-to-deposit ratio is stretched. What follows?

options.t: Little room to lend more without raising deposits, and deposit competition raises funding costs, compressing NIM
The bank will report higher EPS, since it has lent more
The bank must immediately issue bonus shares
NPL will automatically fall

questions.explain: A stretched CD ratio means the bank has already lent out most of what it has taken in. Growing further requires attracting deposits, which means competing on rate, which raises funding costs and compresses net interest margin. This was the central mechanism of the 2021–2023 cycle: the system-wide CD ratio was already stretched when NRB tightened, and fixed deposit rates climbed above 11%.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: If a bank has lent out nearly all its deposits, what must it do to lend more?

questions.stem: A Nepali bank announces a '20% dividend' that is 15% bonus and 5% cash. What goes into a dividend discount model?

options.t: Only the 5% cash portion
The full 20%
Only the 15% bonus portion
The average of the two

questions.explain: A dividend discount model values the cash a shareholder receives, and a bonus share is not cash — it is the same pie in more slices, as Lesson 12.2 established. Using the full 20% overstates intrinsic value by roughly a factor of four and is the most common error people make with this model in Nepal. It is how a valuation model becomes a justification for a decision already made.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which part of that dividend can you actually spend?

questions.stem: In V = D₁ ÷ (r − g), your assumptions give g = 14% and r = 12%. What does that tell you?

options.t: Your assumptions are wrong — growth cannot exceed the required return in this model
The stock is infinitely valuable
The stock is worthless
You should use the absolute value of (r − g)

questions.explain: If g ≥ r the denominator is zero or negative and the formula returns nonsense. The correct response is to revisit the assumptions, not the arithmetic: a company cannot grow its dividend faster than your required return forever, since long-run growth cannot exceed the economy's. Mid single digits for g is defensible; 14% is not. And r should reflect equity risk — if a Nepali fixed deposit paid above 8% at times, demanding 12% for equity is reasonable but 12% against 14% growth is not coherent.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What happens to the fraction when the denominator goes to zero or below?

questions.stem: Your DDM sensitivity table gives a range of Rs. 208 to Rs. 432, and the stock trades at Rs. 496. What have you learned?

options.t: It sits above every defensible cell — worth investigating why
Nothing — the range is too wide to be useful
The stock is definitely overvalued and should be sold short
The model is broken and should be discarded

questions.explain: A price outside the entire range of defensible assumptions is a genuine finding — it means either the market knows something your assumptions do not, or the price is stretched. That is worth investigating. A wide range is not a failure of the model; it is the model telling you honestly how little precision is available. And short selling is not possible on NEPSE in any case.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Inside the range means the model cannot settle it. What does outside the range mean?

questions.stem: A low P/E always means a stock is good value.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False. NBL traded at 7.67× — the lowest P/E of the nineteen commercial banks — with an ROE of 6.76%, below what a Nepali fixed deposit paid during the tightening cycle. It is cheap because it earns poorly. Read P/E next to ROE always: the interesting names are those where a reasonable P/E sits beside a strong ROE, such as KBL at 10.59× with 14.56%.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Cheap relative to what? What is the company actually returning on its capital?

questions.stem: NMB trades at Rs. 233.00 with EPS Rs. 17.10. CZBIL trades at Rs. 194.60 with EPS Rs. 4.63. For every Rs. 1,000 invested, which buys more annual earnings, and by roughly how much?

options.t: NMB — Rs. 73.39 against Rs. 23.80, about three times more
CZBIL — it is Rs. 38.40 cheaper per share
They are roughly equal once you adjust for face value
CZBIL — a higher P/E means more earnings per rupee

questions.explain: Rs. 1,000 ÷ Rs. 233.00 = 4.29 shares × Rs. 17.10 = Rs. 73.39. Rs. 1,000 ÷ Rs. 194.60 = 5.14 shares × Rs. 4.63 = Rs. 23.80. You are not buying a share, you are buying earnings — and NMB delivers about three times more per rupee, from a business with an ROE of 10.34% against CZBIL's 3.14%. The lower share price belongs to the more expensive company.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Work out how many shares Rs. 1,000 buys of each, then multiply by that company's EPS.

questions.stem: Which three ratios predict a Nepali bank's future EPS better than its current P/E? (Select all that apply)

options.t: NPL — non-performing loans as a percentage of total loans
CD ratio — credit to deposit
Net interest margin
Dividend yield

questions.explain: NPL, CD ratio and NIM all describe earnings that have not been reported yet: rising NPL precedes falling EPS by two to four quarters, a stretched CD ratio raises funding costs, and NIM is the core engine. Dividend yield is derived from earnings already reported and from a board decision, so it lags rather than leads. All three of the correct answers are on page one of the quarterly report and on almost no price-tracking site.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these describe the bank's lending book and funding. One describes a payout decision.

questions.stem: NICA traded at a P/E of 343.16× with an ROE of 0.88%. The most likely explanation is:

options.t: Earnings collapsed and the price has not fully adjusted
Investors expect enormous future growth
A calculation error
It is the highest-quality bank in the sector

questions.explain: With EPS at Rs. 1.76 and ROE at 0.88%, the denominator collapsed. A 343× P/E on a near-zero ROE describes a bank that has stopped earning, not one priced for growth. Compare NABIL: P/E 18.40×, EPS Rs. 29.69, ROE 14.86%. Always read P/E with ROE beside it, and treat any P/E above roughly 40× in Nepali banking as a signal to open the quarterly report.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: P/E is price over earnings. Which of those two numbers moved to produce 343×?

questions.stem: Two hydropower projects both quote 10 MW installed capacity. Project A has an annual PLF of 62%, Project B 41%. What does that mean?

options.t: Project A generates about 51% more electricity, and therefore about 51% more revenue at the same tariff
Nothing — installed capacity determines revenue
Project B is more efficient, since it uses less water
They will earn the same, since the PPA tariff is fixed

questions.explain: Installed capacity is a licence to generate up to that much; PLF is what actually gets generated. At the same blended PPA tariff of Rs. 8.40/kWh, 62% PLF produces about Rs. 45.62 crore of annual revenue against about Rs. 30.17 crore at 41% — roughly 51% more. The fixed tariff is exactly why PLF drives the difference: price per unit is set, so volume is everything.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: The tariff per unit is fixed. So what determines revenue?

questions.stem: A hydropower company's Q3 results are much weaker than its Q2. What does that most likely tell you?

options.t: About the weather — compare year-on-year, not sequentially
That the business is deteriorating
That the PPA has been renegotiated downward
That the company has taken on more debt

questions.explain: Most Nepali projects are run-of-river and brutally seasonal: monsoon months run near full capacity while the dry season, roughly Mangsir through Baisakh, can drop generation to a fraction of that. Comparing Q3 to Q2 measures rainfall. Compare Q3 to the same quarter last year, every time. This is the single most common misreading of hydropower financials.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What is different about the river between those two quarters?

questions.stem: What should you check before capacity when evaluating a hydropower company? (Select all that apply)

options.t: Whether a PPA with NEA is signed, and on what terms
The project stage — construction, testing, or post-COD
Debt-to-equity
The number of shares outstanding

questions.explain: A project without a signed Power Purchase Agreement has no route to revenue whatever its capacity. Stage matters because a pre-COD company has no earnings and any 'EPS' figure is close to meaningless. And these are project-finance businesses — target debt-to-equity below 1.0 for an operating company, because a delayed project accrues interest against no revenue and that gap is what destroys equity holders. Share count matters for per-share figures but says nothing about the project.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these determine whether the project can earn anything at all.

questions.stem: Microfinance companies often report ROE above 20%, roughly double the commercial banks. What is that compensating for?

options.t: Unsecured credit risk, borrower over-indebtedness, and heavy regulatory exposure
Nothing — it is simply a better business model
The higher capital adequacy requirement NRB imposes on them
Their lower liquidity on NEPSE

questions.explain: The extra return pays for real risks: lending is small, unsecured and dependent on local conditions; over-indebtedness can maintain apparent repayment until it suddenly cannot; and Nepal Rastra Bank has repeatedly intervened with rate caps, spread caps and dividend restrictions. Crucially those risks are correlated across the whole sector, so a single circular can reprice all 50 listed names at once — which means holding several microfinance companies diversifies almost nothing.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Higher return is usually payment for something. What is being taken on here?

questions.stem: You hold four different microfinance companies. NRB publishes a circular capping the lending spread. What happens?

options.t: All four reprice together — the diversification was across tickers, not risk factors
Only the most leveraged of the four is affected
Nothing, since the circular applies to future lending only
The best-managed company gains market share and rises

questions.explain: The dominant risk in microfinance is regulatory and it applies to every listed name simultaneously. Four companies, one risk factor — the same error as holding five commercial banks, which correlate at about 0.90. And note what makes this sector particularly difficult: there was no company-level warning to read. No NPL trend, no CD ratio deterioration. The risk arrived by circular and hit everyone.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Does the circular distinguish between the four companies?

questions.stem: A non-life insurer grows premiums 18% but its claims ratio rises from 56.1% to 69.8%. How should you read that?

options.t: It wrote much more business and priced it worse — growth without the claims ratio is not information
Excellent — 18% premium growth is the headline that matters
The claims ratio is irrelevant for non-life insurers
Rising claims always indicate fraud

questions.explain: Non-life insurance has a short tail: claims arrive within the year, so the claims ratio is a fast and honest signal about underwriting quality. Premiums up 18% with claims consuming 69.8% rather than 56.1% means the new business was priced badly, or a flood season arrived. Profit fell despite revenue rising, and the solvency margin narrowed — which constrains further growth. Reading growth without the claims ratio is the same error as reading P/E without ROE.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Revenue rose. What happened to the cost of the business that revenue represents?

questions.stem: Why can Nepali insurers act as a diversifier against a bank-heavy portfolio?

options.t: They hold large fixed-deposit floats, so rising rates help them while compressing bank margins
They are not regulated, so policy changes do not affect them
They are more liquid than banks on NEPSE
Their earnings do not depend on the Nepali economy

questions.explain: Insurers invest the float — premiums received but not yet paid out — and in Nepal a large share sits in fixed deposits. So rising interest rates lift investment income at the same time as they compress bank net interest margins. That gives insurance a genuinely different driver from banking. They are regulated (by the Nepal Insurance Authority), they are generally less liquid than the large banks, and they are fully exposed to the domestic economy.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Where do insurers put the premiums they have collected but not yet paid out?

questions.stem: A hotel counter averages Rs. 1.4 lakh of daily turnover. At 10% of a day's volume, what is the largest position you could exit in two trading days, in rupees?
questions.explain: 10% of Rs. 1,40,000 is Rs. 14,000 sellable per day; over two days that is Rs. 28,000. A Rs. 3,00,000 position in the same counter would take about 21 trading days to unwind — during which your own selling pushes the price down. Position size in the thin sectors must be derived from liquidity, not just from your stop. A Rs. 28,000 position you can leave is worth more than a Rs. 3,00,000 one you cannot.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Work out 10% of one day's turnover, then double it for two days.

questions.stem: What advantage do the thin sectors genuinely offer, and to whom?

options.t: Less analysis means mispricings can persist — available only to someone whose horizon matches the illiquidity
Lower commission rates, because turnover is small
More reliable technical patterns, because there is less noise
Faster settlement than the large caps

questions.explain: Thinly-traded companies attract less attention, so genuine mispricings can persist in a way they cannot among the nineteen commercial banks. That is a real edge — but only for someone willing to hold for years without a working exit. Commission is regulated and identical at any turnover, settlement is T+2 for everything, and thin volume makes patterns less reliable, not more.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What is the one thing that is genuinely different about a company nobody is analysing?

questions.stem: Why should you decide your maximum loss in rupees before entering rather than after?

options.t: Once you own it, every decision is contaminated by owning it and by the price you paid
Because SEBON requires a documented risk limit
Because the broker needs it to place the order
Because capital gains tax depends on the stop level

questions.explain: The moment after you buy is the last moment you think clearly about that position. From then on you own it, you have an entry price to anchor to, and loss aversion pushes you to hold losers — all of which Module 15 covers. No regulator or broker requires a stop, and NEPSE does not even offer a stop-loss order type; this is entirely a discipline you impose on yourself, in advance, in writing.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What changes about your thinking the instant you own something?

questions.stem: Ten consecutive losing trades on a Rs. 5,00,000 account. At 2% risk per trade you are down about 18%. At 10% risk, what does the same ten decisions cost?

options.t: About 65%, needing roughly a 186% gain to recover
About 50%, needing a 50% gain
About 100% — the account is wiped out
About 20%, since losses compound slowly

questions.explain: Compounding at 10% per loss leaves 0.9^10 ≈ 34.9% of the account, so down about 65%, requiring roughly +186% to recover. The same ten decisions, the same analysis and the same market produce a survivable 18% at 2% risk and a near-terminal 65% at 10%. Nothing about being right more often would have helped — the only variable that changed was set before entering.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Each loss is taken on the reduced balance. Compound 0.9 ten times.

questions.stem: Your account is Rs. 4,00,000. You risk 1.5% per trade. You want to buy at Rs. 320 with a stop at Rs. 296. How many kitta?
questions.explain: Rupee risk = 4,00,000 × 0.015 = Rs. 6,000. Risk per share = 320 − 296 = Rs. 24. Position = 6,000 ÷ 24 = 250 kitta, costing Rs. 80,000 — 20% of the account, but risking only 1.5%. Exposure and risk are different numbers. Size is derived from the stop; it is never chosen first. Round down to a multiple of 10, and remember that about 1% of round-trip friction makes your real loss closer to Rs. 6,800.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Work out the rupee risk first, then divide by the distance from entry to stop.

questions.stem: You move your stop from Rs. 296 to Rs. 308, keeping the same rupee risk. What happens to the position size?

options.t: It doubles — a tighter stop permits a larger position for the same risk
It halves — a tighter stop means less conviction
It stays the same — size is independent of the stop
It becomes undefined

questions.explain: Risk per share falls from Rs. 24 to Rs. 12, so for the same Rs. 6,000 of risk the position rises from 250 to 500 kitta. This inverts the instinct that a large position is inherently risky: a large position with a close stop and a small position with a distant stop can carry identical risk. What must stay constant is the rupee risk, not the position size.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Rupee risk stays fixed. If risk per share halves, what must happen to the number of shares?

questions.stem: At a 2:1 reward-to-risk ratio, what win rate do you need simply to break even? Answer as a percentage.
questions.explain: Break-even win rate = risk ÷ (reward + risk) = 1 ÷ (2 + 1) = 33.3%. So at 2:1, being right 40% of the time is comfortably profitable. At 1:1 you need 50%, and at 3:1 only 25%. This is why win rate on its own tells you nothing about whether a system makes money — only expectancy does, and expectancy needs both the win rate and the reward-to-risk together.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Divide the risk by the sum of reward and risk.

questions.stem: Trader A wins 40% with +2.5R average wins and −1.0R losses. Trader B wins 70% with +0.6R wins and −1.5R losses. Over 100 trades, who makes money?

options.t: Trader A, at +40R — Trader B loses 3R despite being right far more often
Trader B, because a 70% win rate cannot lose
Both, in roughly equal amounts
Neither — both are net negative after costs

questions.explain: Trader A: (0.4 × 2.5) − (0.6 × 1.0) = +0.40R per trade, or +40R over 100. Trader B: (0.7 × 0.6) − (0.3 × 1.5) = −0.03R, or −3R. Trader B wins nearly twice as often and finishes down, because thirty trades wipe out the seventy. The emotional experience of the two systems is the exact opposite of their results, which is why so few people run the profitable one.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Multiply win rate by average win, then subtract loss rate times average loss, for each.

questions.stem: You lose 50% of your capital. What percentage gain is required to get back to where you started?
questions.explain: G = L ÷ (1 − L) = 0.5 ÷ 0.5 = 100%. The curve is gentle to about 25% and then turns vertical: 20% needs 25%, 50% needs 100%, and 90% needs 900%. This is not psychology, it is arithmetic, and everything in risk management is an attempt to keep you on the flat part of it. The NEPSE index fell 49.5% from its 2021 peak and needed +98.1% to recover.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: If Rs. 100 becomes Rs. 50, what percentage gain takes Rs. 50 back to Rs. 100?

questions.stem: Why does position sizing matter more on NEPSE than on markets with automatic stop-loss orders?

options.t: NEPSE has no stop-loss order type, so if a stock gaps or locks at the −15% circuit you may not get out at your price at all
Because NEPSE charges higher commission on large positions
Because SEBON limits how much any investor may hold in one company
Because T+2 settlement delays all exits by two days

questions.explain: You cannot leave a resting instruction that triggers on a price. Your stop is a decision executed manually inside the 11:00–15:00 session, and a gap or a circuit lock may leave no price at which you can sell that day. Size is the one variable fully under your control, so it carries more of the risk-management load here. Commission is proportional and regulated, and there is no per-investor holding cap.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What happens to your intended stop if the stock locks at the lower circuit?

questions.stem: You hold NABIL, NMB, SANIMA, GBIME and PCBL. How many risk factors do you hold?

options.t: Essentially one — Nepali commercial banking
Five, one per company
Two — large caps and mid caps
Three, grouped by P/E band

questions.explain: All five share the same regulator, the same funding market, the same borrowers, the same interest-rate cycle and the same credit-to-deposit constraint. They correlate at roughly 0.86–0.91 and reprice together the morning NRB publishes a circular. Diversification is across risk factors, not tickers — this is one position wearing five names, and different P/E ratios reflect different earnings, not different risk drivers.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Ask what would have to go wrong for each to fall. Is it the same thing five times?

questions.stem: What is the honest cost of genuinely diversifying a Nepali portfolio away from banking?

options.t: The real diversifiers — hydropower and insurance — are less liquid, so you accept wider spreads and longer exits
There is no cost; diversification is free
Higher commission rates on non-bank sectors
Capital gains tax is higher outside the banking sector

questions.explain: Hydropower correlates at about 0.62 and insurance has a different driver entirely, so both genuinely diversify. Both are also thinner than the large banks, which means wider spreads, longer days-to-exit and less reliable technical analysis. That is a real trade-off — and it is usually still worth paying, provided you size the illiquid positions from their liquidity rather than from conviction. Commission and CGT are identical across sectors.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Where do the genuine diversifiers sit on NEPSE, and what is true about their turnover?

questions.stem: Holding twelve companies is necessarily more diversified than holding five.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False. Twelve companies across one risk factor is less diversified than five across four. Past about eight to ten genuinely different holdings, additional names add little and cost attention. And most Nepali investors carry a concentration nobody counts: salary, family income, property and portfolio all exposed to the same domestic economy — which makes the portfolio a smaller share of total household risk than it appears, and correlated with the rest of it.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Count risk factors, not tickers.

questions.stem: Put the five stages of a bubble in order, as NEPSE ran them between 2019 and 2023.
items: Displacement — NRB cuts rates, liquidity is abundant, MeroShare removes account-opening friction
Boom — prices rise on real reasons and early buyers make real money
Euphoria — new participants cannot name what the company does, margin lending expands
Distribution — the index goes sideways at a high level while individual stocks stop making new highs
Panic — NRB tightens, FD rates pass 11%, margin unwinds, and the index falls 49.5%
questions.explain: The sequence repeats because the human process does. What matters most is stage 2: the boom is indistinguishable from a healthy bull market, because it is one. And stage 4 is invisible from inside — distribution feels like consolidation, and everyone is still bullish. At every stage the crowd was rational given what it believed; the failure was the absence of a rule written down before the emotion arrived.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Something real starts it, and something real ends it. The middle three are about who is buying.

questions.stem: Which are the reliable late-cycle warning signs? (Select all that apply)

options.t: New Demat account growth accelerating
Low-quality names outperforming the leaders
Margin lending expanding faster than the index
The index making a new all-time high

questions.explain: Accelerating account growth means the last buyers are arriving; junk outperforming leaders means the good ideas ran out — visible as the headline NEPSE index outrunning the Sensitive Index, which Lesson 2.4 covered; and rising leverage is the fuel that must eventually unwind. A new high is not a warning sign at all: every bull market makes them, and most are followed by more. None of the three tell you the exact top; all of them tell you to reduce position size and stop adding.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these describe who is buying and with what. One is just a price.

questions.stem: Why is NEPSE structurally more prone to overshooting than markets with two-sided participation?

options.t: There is no short selling, so scepticism can only be expressed by staying out
The ±15% circuit amplifies moves
T+2 settlement forces investors to hold longer
Because SEBON restricts institutional participation

questions.explain: With no short selling, there is no mechanism for sceptics to express a view and dampen a rise — sentiment can only be expressed by buying or by staying out. Combined with a heavy retail base and 91 thinly-traded hydropower counters, that makes overshoot more likely in both directions. The circuit limits daily movement rather than amplifying it, and T+2 restrains churn rather than encouraging overshoot.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: How does someone who thinks a stock is overpriced express that view on NEPSE?

questions.stem: What single question cuts through the 'long-term investor' rationalisation?

options.t: If I did not already own this, would I buy it today at this price?
How far is it from its all-time high?
How long have I held it?
What did I pay for it?

questions.explain: That question removes your history from the decision, which is exactly what the rationalisation depends on. If the answer is yes, holding is a real decision; if no, you are not holding — you are avoiding the act of selling. The other three questions all reference your past or the stock's, and the market knows nothing about either. Being a long-term investor is legitimate when chosen in advance, with a horizon and a rationale; becoming one after a 40% fall is a different thing wearing the same words.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which question would you ask about a stock you had never owned?

questions.stem: You average down three times on a falling position. It began as 20% of your account. What is the usual outcome?

options.t: A position far past your size limit, with no stop, decided in pieces rather than as one choice
A lower average cost with unchanged risk
A guaranteed recovery, since the break-even price is now lower
Reduced exposure, since you bought at cheaper prices

questions.explain: Averaging down lowers your average cost and raises your total exposure to a position moving against you — the opposite of what your risk rules said. Each purchase feels reasonable in isolation, which is the mechanism: nobody decides to put 57% of an account into one counter, but three separate decisions can arrive there. The break-even price falls but the amount at stake rises, so the rupee loss required to reach it grows.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Average cost went down. What happened to the total amount committed?

questions.stem: Two people own the same share at Rs. 300 today. One paid Rs. 180, the other Rs. 420. What is the correct decision input?

options.t: The company's current numbers — the entry price is relevant only to tax and sizing
Each person's entry price, since it determines their profit
The higher of the two entry prices, as a fair reference
The Rs. 100 face value

questions.explain: Both hold identical assets with identical futures. Your entry price is a fact about your history, not about the company, and the market has no idea what it is. It matters for exactly two things: computing capital gains tax, and knowing your position size. Face value is an accounting convention that says nothing about value at all — it is simply the second anchor Nepali investors carry.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Does the company behave differently for one owner than the other?

questions.stem: Knowing about anchoring does not stop you feeling it. What actually works?

options.t: Procedure — write the exit before entry, and evaluate the company before looking at what you paid
Willpower and self-awareness
Checking the price more frequently
Setting a mental target and remembering it

questions.explain: Anchoring is not a knowledge problem — the feeling is produced before the reasoning arrives, so understanding it completely does not remove the pull. What works is procedural: decide the exit in advance, review positions on their current merits, and look at your entry price only afterwards and only for tax and sizing. Checking more often increases exposure to the anchor, and a mental target is precisely the kind of commitment that gets renegotiated when it becomes inconvenient.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: If the feeling arrives before the reasoning, what kind of solution can help?

questions.stem: Which of these are warning signs of a coordinated pump? (Select all that apply)

options.t: The tip names a target price but no scenario in which it fails
Volume in a thin counter rises sharply days before any news
The message urges you to buy before it is too late
The company published its quarterly results on its own website

questions.explain: The first three are the standard structure: quiet accumulation, a seeded tip with urgency and no downside case, then retail buying that organisers distribute into. Published quarterly results are ordinary, mandatory disclosure — the opposite of a warning sign. SEBON prohibits market manipulation; if you see this pattern the correct response is to stay out and report it, not to try to time an exit ahead of organisers who are already ahead of you.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Three of these describe how a tip arrives. One describes a company obeying disclosure rules.

questions.stem: Why do pump organisers deliberately choose thin counters?

options.t: Little buying moves the price a lot — and the same thin liquidity traps retail buyers when they try to leave
Thin counters have lower commission rates
SEBON does not monitor thin counters
Thin counters are exempt from the circuit limit

questions.explain: On a counter trading Rs. 2 lakh a day, modest buying moves the price sharply — which makes the accumulation cheap and the apparent confirmation dramatic. The same thinness is what traps buyers in the final stage: exiting a Rs. 2,00,000 position at 10% of a Rs. 3 lakh daily turnover takes roughly seven trading days, with your own selling pushing the price lower. It was never an accident that a thin counter was chosen. Commission, monitoring and circuit limits are identical everywhere.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Think about both ends: what does thin liquidity do when they buy, and when you try to sell?

questions.stem: What makes a trading rule testable?

options.t: Two people reading it would take the same action on the same chart
It has produced a profit over the last six months
It is based on a well-known indicator
It can be written in one sentence

questions.explain: That is the whole standard. 'Buy good stocks when they are cheap' fails it — everyone agrees and no two people would buy the same thing. 'Buy when the 20-day SMA crosses above the 50-day and 20-day average turnover exceeds Rs. 50 lakh' passes, because both conditions are checkable in a minute by anyone. Past profit does not make a rule testable, a famous indicator does not make it specific, and brevity is not precision.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Hand your rule to a stranger. Would they buy the same thing you would?

questions.stem: Which rule should come first on NEPSE, before any entry criterion?

options.t: The liquidity filter — a floor on 20-day average turnover
The entry signal
The profit target
The indicator set

questions.explain: Apply the liquidity filter before you look at a chart, and a large share of the 271 listed companies disappears from your universe — which is the correct outcome, since they are not tradeable at retail size with a stop. Lesson 11.5 showed a liquidity filter outperforming six indicators. Entry rules get all the attention and matter least; the liquidity filter, the stop and the size do most of the work.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which rule removes the most bad trades before you have even looked at a price?

questions.stem: Which journal column does the most work, and why?

options.t: The one-line thesis — writing it before entry prevents some trades from happening at all
The exit price, since it determines profit
The date, since it shows trading frequency
The symbol, since it reveals concentration

questions.explain: Forcing yourself to state the reason in one sentence before entering exposes the trades that have no reason — a thesis reading 'it's been going up' tends not to survive being written down. That preventive effect is most of the journal's value, more than the review it enables. The other columns are all genuinely useful; date shows frequency, symbol reveals concentration, and exit in R lets you compute expectancy.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which column is filled in before the trade rather than after?

questions.stem: Why should outcomes be recorded in R rather than in rupees?

options.t: R makes trades comparable across different position sizes and lets you compute expectancy directly
Because rupee amounts are affected by capital gains tax
Because R is required for tax filing
Because rupee figures are harder to remember

questions.explain: An R-multiple expresses each outcome as a multiple of what was risked, so a Rs. 4,000 gain on a Rs. 2,000 risk and a Rs. 20,000 gain on a Rs. 10,000 risk are both +2R and directly comparable. That is what lets you evaluate a system rather than a story, and compute expectancy across trades of different sizes. Nothing about R relates to tax filing, which uses actual rupee gains and your WACC.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: How would you compare a small trade and a large one fairly?

questions.stem: Your monthly review shows +0.31R expectancy but two rule-breaks out of nine trades, one losing −2.2R. What should you change?

options.t: Nothing about the system — fix the execution
The entry rules, since the system clearly is not working
The position sizing, to reduce the largest loss
Everything — start again with a different approach

questions.explain: A system producing +0.31R expectancy is working. The −2.2R loss exceeded the maximum a −1R stop should allow, which means a stop was moved or skipped — an execution failure, not a design failure. Separating 'the system lost money' from 'I did not follow the system' is the point of the review, because they have opposite remedies. Most people conclude the first when the truth is the second, and end up rewriting a system that was fine.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Was the loss larger than the system permitted, or was the system's design wrong?

questions.stem: Why must a monthly review include costs and tax in the R calculation?

options.t: Otherwise the review is systematically optimistic — a +0.15R gross system can be net zero after 1% friction and 10% short-term CGT
Because SEBON requires cost-adjusted performance reporting
Because costs vary between brokers
Because R-multiples cannot be computed without tax figures

questions.explain: Every round trip costs roughly 1% in commission, SEBON fee and two DP charges, and short-term gains have been taxed at 10% since 17 July 2026. A system showing a small gross edge may be net negative — which is exactly the finding a review exists to surface. No regulator requires this of a private investor; commission is regulated and identical across brokers; and R is computable gross or net, which is precisely why you must be explicit about which you are using.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What has been deducted before the money reaches you, and is it in your R figures?

questions.stem: Twenty trades is enough to judge whether a system works.

options.t: True
False

questions.explain: False. At a 50% win rate, runs of five consecutive losses are entirely ordinary, and twenty trades can easily produce a misleading result in either direction. Look for patterns across months rather than verdicts within one. And when you do change something, change one thing at a time — change two rules simultaneously and you cannot attribute the result to either.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: How unusual is a run of five losses at a 50% win rate?

questions.stem: In the 90-day plan, what defines success at day 90?

options.t: A complete journal, zero rule-breaks, and no position that risked more than 2%
A profit on the account
At least ten completed trades
Beating the NEPSE index over the period

questions.explain: Ninety days is far too short a sample for profit to mean anything either way — Lesson 16.3 made the point that even twenty trades cannot settle it. What ninety days can establish is whether you can follow a process: a complete journal, no rule-breaks, and disciplined sizing. Get those right and returns become a question of time and sample size; get them wrong and no amount of analysis rescues it. More trades is the opposite of the goal — the plan caps you at three.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: What can ninety days actually prove, and what can it not?

questions.stem: The plan requires real positions of Rs. 25,000 or more. Why that floor?

options.t: Below it, flat charges dominate — a Rs. 1,000 trade needs a 5.77% move just to break even
Because brokers refuse orders below Rs. 25,000
Because the minimum lot is 10 kitta
Because capital gains tax only applies above Rs. 25,000

questions.explain: The Rs. 25 DP charge is flat and you pay it on both legs, so it is 2.5% of a Rs. 1,000 trade and 0.01% of a Rs. 2,30,000 one. Keeping positions at roughly Rs. 25,000 or above holds round-trip friction under about 1%. No broker imposes such a minimum, the 10-kitta lot is unrelated, and CGT applies to any gain regardless of size.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which of the three charges does not scale with trade size, and how many times do you pay it?

questions.stem: Two learners are both down 2.1% after 90 days. Learner A took 3 documented trades with zero rule-breaks and paid Rs. 2,240 in costs. Learner B took 11 trades, documented 4, broke rules 5 times, and paid Rs. 9,870. What is the real difference?

options.t: Learner A has data to learn from; Learner B paid four times as much to find out nothing
No difference — the returns are identical
Learner B gained more experience by taking more trades
Learner A was simply luckier

questions.explain: At ninety days a 2.1% loss is noise and says nothing about either approach. Learner A can compute an expectancy, see which rules helped, and carry that forward. Learner B cannot tell whether their system works because they did not run one — and will be in the same position in another ninety days, having paid another Rs. 10,000 to learn nothing. Volume of trades is not experience if none of it is recorded. The account balance is the least informative number on the table.
questions.hintOnFirstWrong: Which of the two can answer the question 'does my system work?' at the end of the period?
